subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext:
The House proceeded to the consideration of an amendment made by the Senate to Bill C-14, an Act for granting to Her Majesty certain sums of money for the Government of Canada for the financial year ending March 31, 1990.
May 15, 1989

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government's interim supply Bill for 1989-90, Bill C-14, was approved by this House on May 4, 1989. The Bill has been reported from the other place with an amendment which states that the four special warrants signed by the Governor General earlier this year shall be deemed to have been legal. This House must now decide whether to agree or disagree with this amendment.
On the surface, the proposed amendment appears innocent, but it is not so. This amendment suggests that the actions taken by the Government through the use of special Governor General's warrants earlier this year were indeed illegal. This inference is wrong.
The request for special warrants and their approval on my recommendation by the Governor General was fully consistent with the laws approved by Parliament. When the Bill was reviewed in the other place, its legal counsel stated that the Government's actions were fully consistent with the laws approved by Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want there to be any doubt on this matter. The record shows clearly that the Government's actions were proper and legal.
To accept the amendment would imply that Ministers of this Government have acted illegally. To accept the amendment would be to suggest that the actions taken under an Act of Parliament were illegal. To accept the amendment is to imply that the Governor General acted contrary to the law. The amendment referred to this House is not an innocent minor change.
Over the past few days, as this matter has been debated in the other place, fact and opinion have tended to be mixed together, creating confusion and uncertainty. I want to ensure that the facts about the use of special warrants are clearly on the record.

I would first like to review the circumstance surrounding the Government's use of special warrants. As most Hon. Members know, the second session of the Thirty Third Parliament had met almost continuously for 24 months before being dissolved for the General Election of November 21. After the election, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) convened Parliament a mere three weeks later in order to complete the business of the
Appropriation Act
previous Parliament on which the people of Canada had spoken out so clearly and convincingly.
It has been a long time since Parliament has been convened so quickly after an election. Certainly, no Prime Minister in the last 40 years has convened Parliament within three weeks of a General Election. The opening session of the new Parliament, as the Speech from the Throne on December 12 made clear, was to deal with the free trade legislation. Once the free trade legislation was approved, the House agreed to adjourn on December 30.

The Government on December 16 did table Supplementary Estimates "B" for the 1988-89 fiscal year, clearly informing this House of its need for further supply for that fiscal year.
As supply had not been dealt with when the House adjourned, the Government requested the Governor General to approve special warrants. Section 30 of the Financial Administration Act provides that special warrants may be approved when the House is adjourned.
Let me turn directly to the question of legality which is raised by the proposed amendment. Parliament has provided a process for the continuing and orderly operation of government when it is not sitting. That is the fundamental essence of Section 30 of the Financial Administration Act: to provide interim funding so that the business of government can continue uninterrupted until Parliament is able to deal with the important matter of supply.
Section 30 of the Financial Administration Act cites three criteria which must be satisfied before special Governor General's warrants can be drawn: first, Parliament is not in session; second, there are no available appropriations from which to satisfy these requirements; and third, there are payments which are urgently required for the public good.

The first condition which must be satisfied is that Parliament is not in session. There is no dispute that Parliament was not in session. However, I would like to clarify an important point about how the Financial Administration Act defines not in session. Section 30, paragraph (5) states without any qualifications or conditions that Parliament is deemed to be not in session when it is under adjournment. This section was tabled in 1951 explicitly to enable the Government to obtain special Governor General's warrants that are required when Parliament is under adjournment. The Parliament

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
of the day clearly intended that special Governor General's warrants would be issued under this provision.
It is reasonable to assume that when Parliament amends an Act such as as the Financial Administration Act, it expects and accepts that it will be used. As the Speaker stated in the House on May 2 of this year, there is no inference that the words "not in session" were to be restricted to dissolution periods.
The second condition that no other appropriations are available is a factual determination. I assure Hon. Members that there were no other appropriations available to meet these obligations.
The third condition requires that there is a payment urgently required for the public good. The interpretation of this section has received much attention in recent weeks. I would like to assure Hon. Members that the interpretation of this section used by the Government was consistent with all previous requests since 1896 for the issuance of special warrants by the Governor General.
In reviewing the use of special warrants, the other place has attached a novel interpretation to the concept of urgency. It has associated that concept with the state of Parliament's condition, suggesting that a distinction is required according to whether Parliament is dissolved, prorogued or adjourned. The condition of urgency provided for in Section 30 is related to the payment that must be made, not to the varying states in which this House may be at any particular time.
The counsel to the other place did advise that it was improper to imply in an amendment that the actions taken under a provision of the law which had been complied with would be illegal. In other words, there is no basis for making legal what is already legal. The flaw
in the proposed amendment cannot be stated any clearer.

I would now like to address the matter of how Parliament has been kept informed. In every instance that warrants were issued, there was an almost immediate reference in the Canada Gazette. For example, the January 19 warrant was gazetted on January 28, well in advance of the 30-day requirement established by the Financial Administration Act. Furthermore, on April 12, one week before the required date, I tabled in thise House a statement for the 1988-89 fiscal year which provided to Parliament more disclosure than had ever been provided before about how the warrants were used.
Mr. Speaker, the matter before us requires resolution today. The special warrant signed by Her Excellency the Governor General on April 1 was intended to cover the Government's requirements for the first 45 days of this fiscal year. It was expected that this could allow time for Parliament to consider and approve the interim supply bill.
The House has certainly lived up to its responsibilities and, as agreed by all Parties on April 4, the House approved interim supply on May 4, one week after the Main Estimates were presented.
Failure to receive Royal Assent for Bill C-14 today will require that the Government cease to make payments from appropriations to be voted for any goods to be received, services to be rendered or benefits to be provided after midnight tonight.
This will mean that a number of government suppliers may not receive on time the payments which they have earned. What will be the consequences for businesses which rely on receiving these payments?
Mr. Speaker, Canadian veterans may experience delay in receiving their pension and allowance payments. Canada's debt to our veterans is surely sufficiently great that we should not create the anguish that a delay in payment may cause many of them.
Members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are scheduled to receive their bi-weekly pay cheques by the end of this week. We expect them to maintain our national security and law enforcement at all times. Their remuneration should not be delayed for a "very small point", to quote an Honourable Member of the other place.
May 15, 1989



This is an important matter that requires our immediate action, Mr. Speaker. The Government is interested in ensuring that those who have earned their payments receive them from the federal Government in the timely manner which they have anticipated. I have established, Mr. Speaker, that there is no question of impropriety or illegality. I accept the opinion advanced by the legal counsel of the other place:
The law according to its own term has been complied with.
Accordingly, the Government is not prepared to accept the proposed amendment. I recommend that this House send the following motion back to the other place.
I move, seconded by the Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), the following motion:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this House disagrees with the amendment made by the Senate to Bill C-14, An Act for granting to Her Majesty certain sums of money for the Government of Canada for the financial year ending 31st March, 1990, because this House believes that the special warrants signed by the Governor General on January 19, February 16, March 23 and April 1, 1989 are already legal.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands (Mr. Milliken).

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on the Minister's motion concerning the amendment proposed by the other place to Bill C-14. I believe that the amendment proposed is good and necessary and should be passed by this House for the reasons I shall give now.

The motion, in my view, is essential to the rights of Parliament, that is, the amendment that has been proposed by the Senate and that this motion seeks to destroy. In my submission, what we are discussing here today is fundamental to the rights of this House and to Parliament in general. It is a subject on which I have spoken several times in this House during the course of this session on questions of privilege and on points of order. Mr. Speaker, with your indulgence, I would like to
Appropriation Act
review some of the events that have led up to the discussion we are having today.
The principle on which we are operating in this Chamber is that of the supremacy of Parliament. While it may seem tedious to go back to certain authorities on this subject, in my submission, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) needs some assistance in his attempts to determine the intent and meaning of the amendment that has been proposed by the Senate in this case. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis) says, "No". But I would like to refer to higher authorities, and I have some here. I am sure he will recognize some of them. I would like to turn first to the late A. V. Dicey's book called An Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution. I am referring to Tenth Edition, 1959, page 69. Mr. Speaker, the learned author says:
Parliament can legally legislate on any topic whatever which, in the judgment of Parliament, is a fit subject for legislation. There is not power which, under the English constitution, can come into rivalry with the legislative sovereignty of Parliament.
No one of the limitations alleged to be imposed by law on the absolute authority of Parliament has any real existence, or receives any countenance, either from the statute-book or from the practice of the courts.
This doctrine of the legislative supremacy of Parliament is the very keystone of the law of the Constitution.
I repeat, "the very keystone of the law of the Constitution". It is my submission, Mr. Speaker, that what the Government is doing here today is tampering with that keystone.
The concept of the supremacy of Parliament is not one that just happened overnight. It was developed in the United Kingdom and transported to this country over hundreds of years.
Dicey, in his learned treatise, in a footnote on page 69, deals with part of the historical reason why Parliament got control of expenditure and revenue. I would like to read part of the footnote from page 69:
The historical reason why Parliament has never succeeded in passing immutable laws, or in other words, has always retained its character of a supreme legislature, lies deep in the history of the English people and in the peculiar development of the English constitution. England has, at any rate since the Norman Conquest, been always governed by an absolute legislator.
This lawgiver was originally the Crown, and the peculiarity of the process by which the English constitution has been developed lies in the fact that the legislative authority of the Crown has never been curtailed, but has been transferred from the Crown acting alone (or rather in council) to the Crown acting first together with, and then in subordination to, the Houses of Parliament. Hence Parliament, or

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
in technical terms the Queen in Parliament, has become-it would
perhaps be better to say has always remained-a supreme
legislature.
This notion of Parliament having supremacy was determined on the basis of expenditure and revenue. It was determined in the course of a series of struggles between Parliament and the King. I need not go into all the historical details, but I can remind Hon. Members-perhaps the Minister of Justice will be interested to hear this. I will save that deeper aspect for another day.
The transfer of these powers took place in the course of a lengthy struggle which culminated in a civil war in the United Kingdom which started in 1642. Hon. Members will recall that the struggle in that civil war was between Parliament, which claimed to have control over the expenditure and the revenue-gathering functions of the state, as against the King. King Charles I ultimately lost his head as a result of that struggle in 1649. At that time Parliament essentially gained control of the pursestrings, a control which it has tightened up over the years since that time. I do not pretend that things have not changed since 1649, heaven knows they have, but the changes, I submit, are important only in the sense that the principle has been left untouched and, if anything, has been strengthened.
Why did Parliament go for the purse-strings? Because the legislators in Parliament in those days, as today, know that the person who pays the piper calls the tune. The person with control of the money effectively controls the Government. The situation in England was a little different. It had a king who happened to have a lot of manorial interests. He owned a lot of estates and lands and had various means by which he could raise money without resorting to parliamentary approval. He got that money in and he paid the money out without the authority of Parliament.
As time went on and as the role of Government grew in society, the revenues that the king derived from these sources became smaller and smaller as a percentage of the total requirements of the Government, so further recourse was had to Parliament to raise money by way of taxation. As soon as that authority was requested,
Parliament began attaching conditions to the granting of money to the Crown.
That procedure was transported to Canada when this country was established. Our forbears struggled for and obtained the notion and principle of responsible Government in the legislatures of the various provinces of Canada before Confederation. That principle of responsible Government requires that the Government be responsible and report to the legislature, and that its spending plans and priorities be introduced in and be adopted by the legislature prior to the expenditure of public funds.
I would like to turn to authorities on this point that describe the financial relationship between the Crown and Parliament. I would refer to Beauchesne's Sixth Edition, 1989, page 183, citation 595. Basically, it is a direct quotation from Erskine May's book which I will be referring to presently. The citation has been amended in Beauchesne's to reflect the Canadian experience. It states:
The Crown, being the executive power, has the responsibility for the raising and spending of money. Acting through responsible Ministers, the Crown makes known to the Commons the financial necessities of Government. The Commons grants such aids and supplies as are necessary to meet the demands of the Crown and provides through taxes and other sources of revenue the ways and means to meet the supplies that have been granted. The Crown, therefore, demands money, the Commons grants it and the Senate assents to the grant. The Commons does not vote any money except for the necessities of the country as defined by the Crown.
Clearly the responsibility for determining the necessities of the country lies with the Government. That is undisputed and that is why we have the Royal Recommendation as a requirement on all the money bills that come to this House.
The statement of the law that is laid down in Beauchesne's reflects not only the Statutes of Canada, but also the constitutional practice which is very much a part of our laws.
I turn now to Erskine May, twentieth edition, and a paragraph very similar to the one I quoted, but instead of referring to the Senate it refers to the House of Lords. At page 750 Erskine May describes in more detail the nature of this relationship between the Crown and Parliament. The learned author writes:

The financial relations between the Crown and Parliament defined in the preceding paragraph took shape during the period while the King still governed through ministers responsible to himself, and the House of Commons only exercised a negative control through its power to withhold supplies. These constitutional relations have been maintained in essential continuity, despite the establishment of Cabinet government dependent upon the support of the House of Commons. In the Cabinet, powers derived from two different sources are combined without being confounded. As Ministers of the Crown, its members initiate policy and conduct administration. As leaders of the majority of the House of Commons, they secure authorization of their policy through their influence over their supporters.
Over questions of financial policy it may be that the influence of ministers normally avails to reduce the House's power of control to a right to criticize, exercised chiefly by the Opposition. But the twofold powers concentrated in the Cabinet-the one group exercised in virtue of statute or the prerogative, the other based on convention-
And I stress the words "based on convention".
-are alike contingent on the continued support of the House of
Commons and liable to be forfeited through the loss of that support.
At page 751 he states:
The financial control of the House of Commons is exercised at two different levels. As an agent in the formation of policy, it authorizes the several objects of expenditure and the sums to be spent on each; it also authorizes the levying of taxes. On the level of administration, it satisfies itself that its expenditure decisions are duly carried out-in other words, that the sums it has granted, and no more, are spent for the purposes for which they were granted, and for no other purposes. For both sets of functions the House of Commons has, partly through its own procedure, and partly through legislation and administrative practice, secured appropriate machinery.
The procedure and machinery for the control of financial policy-the presentation of estimates, the budget, the voting of estimates, the business of Ways and Means-form the subjects of the chapters that follow.
The learned author is clearly describing the way in which the House performs its basic, fundamental and very important constitutional functions in relation to the control of expenditure and taxation.
Another paragraph which may be of interest is on page 761. Again, the learned author is discussing relations between Parliament and the Crown. That paragraph states:
Financial practice began to take shape during the long period when the King enjoyed a non-parliamentary revenue which was expected to provide for the ordinary needs of government, and when no legal
Appropriation Act
sanction fettered his discretion in disposing of the supplementary revenue granted by Parliament. During all this period the Commons, as a body traditionally in favour of royal economy, naturally abstained from taking the initiative in offering money to the Crown. The practice of demand preceding grant had accordingly solidified into an invariable rule before Parliament began to take steps to appropriate its grants to the purposes for which they were demanded. Hence, in the matter of Supply, no Standing Order of the House of Commons was necessary to maintain the principle of the financial initiative of the Crown.
When, with the commencement of parliamentary control over the Exchequer, the granting of Supply was differentiated into two functions-the votings of sums of money and the provision of revenue by taxation-it was accepted without question by the House of Commons that the rule applied to both of the now clearly distinguished functions of Supply and of Whys and Means, and to any business which belonged to either of those classes.
The precedents concerning the control of finance in the House of Commons go back hundreds of years. We would do well to regard those precedents as binding in Canada under our constitutional practice. While they may not be codified in any particular place, nevertheless, in my submission, they are clearly part of our law.
I would now turn to more recent times. Mr. Speaker made a ruling, reported in Hansard of May 2, 1989, at page 1176 which contains a description of the Canadian practice in relation to the granting of supply.
I want to read two paragraphs of that ruling because I think they accurately state the current law in Canada:
The House of Commons has an important role to play in this complicated process.
He is talking about the process of Supply:
It is in the Commons where the Government's projected expenditures-known as the "Estimates"-are first tabled and the legislation to implement the estimates-known as the "Appropriation" Bill-is introduced. Section 53 of the Constitution Act, 1867 stipulates that all financial legislation, and this includes Government expenditures, must originate in the House of Commons. This requirement is reaffirmed in the Commons's own rules of procedure, more specifically Standing Order 80(1), a point which was clearly referred to by Hon. Members the other day.
As a result of the fact that Main Estimates for the upcoming fiscal year are usually adopted at the end of June, the Government could be without funds from the beginning of the fiscal year in April to the end of June.
The rules accordingly provide for the Government to request an advance against the Main Estimates which is known as Interim Supply. From time to time during a session, the Government may

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
also require additional funds which are introduced by way of Supplementary Estimates.
In this case, as we will see in a moment, we had Main Estimates introduced but only after the Government had dished out to itself some $6 billion of the money that was contained in those Estimates by special warrants.
In his ruling, Mr. Speaker referred to Section 53 of the Constitution Act. I will read it again. Section 53 provides:
Bills for appropriating any Part of the Public Revenue, or for imposing any Thx or Impost, shall originate in the House of Commons.
There is no dispute that the Chair agrees with that. I am sure the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) agrees with that. It is part of the law of Canada.
The Financial Administration Act is the Act upon which the Government is relying for the procedure that it has followed in respect of these special warrants. I want to take a moment again to refer Hon. Members to Sections of that Act because the Minister referred to them in his speech this morning. I think it would be more clear if the Act were read in detail. Section 26 of the Financial Administration Act provides as follows:
Subject to the Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982, no payments shall be made out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund without the authority of Parliament.
The Financial Administration Act itself contains that provision for no spending without parliamentary authority. Yet the Government is spending by special warrants. Where is the authority?
The Minister relies on Section 30 of the Financial Administration Act. To be fair, I will read the relevant provisions of Section 30. Section 30(1) states:
Where a payment is urgently required for the public good when Parliament is not in session and there is no other appropriation pursuant to which the payment may be made, the Governor in Council, on the report of the President of the Treasury Board that there is no appropriation for the payment and the report of the appropriate Minister that the payment is urgently required for the public good, may, by order, direct the preparation of a special warrant to be signed by the Governor General authorizing the payment to be made out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
I will skip to Section 30(5) because I do not believe the other provisions are relevant.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Read it all.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Hon. Members would like to hear the whole thing. I will send them a copy.
Section 30(5) provides:
For the purposes of this section, Parliament shall be deemed to be not in session when it is under adjournment sine die-
These words the Minister left out from his quote of the Section:
-or to a day more than two weeks after the day the Governor in Council made the order directing the preparation of the special warrant.
I will return to those words because in my submission Section 30(5) is essential to an understanding of the reason for the amendment that the Senate has proposed to this Bill.
Resort has been had to the Financial Administration Act or its predecessors over the years. The earliest precedent that we have been able to determine is 1896.1 think that is common ground on both sides.
The Minister has given evidence before a committee of the other place on this matter. I am sure he is as aware of the precedents as I am, if not more aware.
The fact is that in all the cases where these warrants have been used, save one, they were used during the time between the dissolution of Parliament and the commencement of a new Parliament, not a new session or a different session, but a new Parliament.
As I understand the precedents, the only case where it did not happen was in 1896, when urgent repairs were needed for a leaky roof.
What we are faced with here today is something quite unprecedented. As I have said on numerous occasions during the course of discussion on this Bill and in my question of privilege on April 6, this is a case where the Government is using Governor General's special warrants to meet ordinary pay day requirements, and using them between the times that Parliament has met and is available to deal with the business of Supply.
I think the facts of this case are most important. I want to turn to Clause 3 of Bill C-14, which refers to the date upon which these special warrants were issued. There were several warrants that were offensive in the sense that we are discussing this morning. A warrant was issued on January 19, on February 16 and March 23, 1989. Those were in the last financial year. Then an
May 15, 1989

additional warrant for about $6 billion was issued on April 1.
The Government itself is seeking confirmation of the original three warrants in this Bill under Clause 3. In effect, it is acknowledging that if there was any impropriety with respect to the issue of those warrants, it is being cleared up by this Bill.
The Bill does not deal with the special warrant issued on April 1. I suppose if there were varying degrees of impropriety, I would rank this as the most gross distortion of the practice that has arisen in respect of this matter.
This procedure is totally unprecedented. I raised the matter in the House on April 6, five days after the issue of the warrant. I gave notice to Mr. Speaker of my intention to raise the matter if not two days before, the day before early in the morning.
The matter was also raised by me on three occasions in one way or another on May 4, the day the Bill was passed in the House. I only refer to the discussion that took place on that day to say that on no occasion has the Government cited any precedents to support the actions that it has taken in respect of this matter. Every time I have raised this matter I have been told that whatever the Government has done was in accordance with past practices, yet not one example of that past practice has been cited in the House in support of the position the Government is taking in this matter. There was not one cited today and there has not been one cited in any other place that I am aware of. I can understand why. It is totally unprecedented. It is new, and I suggest that it is wrong. It goes contrary to the general thrust of our constitutional practice.
In this case the Bill was passed in accordance with a special order on May 4 and went to the other place for consideration, for some sober second thought. I can only say that I think that sober second thought is extremely important in consideration of this matter.
The suggestion that the Senate amendment to this Bill somehow suggests illegality is unfair. I believe that what the other place has sought to do is clear up any ambiguity that may have arisen because of the use of these warrants. In order to justify the use of these warrants, the President of the Treasury Board must be relying on Section 30(1) and 30(5) of the Financial Administration Act.
Appropriation Act
This matter has been discussed in the House before and Mr. Speaker made a ruling. I want to refer again to page 1179 of Hansard of May 2. Mr. Speaker said:
As to the argument that the law has been breached, Hon. Members have other avenues available to them to demonstrate and establish those facts.
Mr. Speaker left open the question whether there had been a breach of the Financial Administration Act and of the Constitution Act in dealing with these warrants. I suggest that one of the other avenues Mr. Speaker may have had in mind is the other place. Clearly, there was a group of men and women who were receptive to the idea that there had been some hanky-panky. There are other avenues, and another avenue has been pursued. I suggest it is an avenue that has yielded some good results.
We have the Minister today telling us that the other avenue, as he intends it, is in court. Why should we as Members of Parliament have to go to court to defend the rights of this place? This is the highest court in the land. Surely we should not have to run down to the Supreme Court to obtain a ruling to see whether or not the Government has acted illegally. Surely, we should be able to determine that here.
I ask the Government to look at this amendment again. I ask the Government to look at it in a different light. Do not look at it as a criticism of what it has done. Look at it as a constructive attempt to correct what may or may not be an error.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Say that with a straight face.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Hon. Members may laugh. They are laughing at the rights of Parliament being trampled upon in this case.
We say that this amendment is reasonable. We say that there is a risk that what the Government has done in this case is illegal. We ought not to be putting in uncertainty by passing an Act in this House, or even in the other place, that does not deal with the ambiguity that has been created by the actions of Government.
I would like to look at the reasons why we believe the Minister may have-and I stress the words "may have"-acted improperly in granting these warrants. The fundamental principle of our Constitution, as I have indicated, is that it is this House, and Parliament in particular that retains control of expenditures. What has happened here is the Government tabled Supplementary Estimates on December 16. Those Estimates effectively provided for the provision of additional moneys to the Government for purposes that had not been approved by Parliament. It then gave itself those moneys by way of special warrants between the sessions of Parliament. In

Appropriation Act
other words, without having the House of Commons or a single committee spend a single day looking at any of the Supplementary Estimates the Government decided that those Estimates were as good as law and it had Her Excellency sign a special warrant. The Government took that money out of the Public Treasury and spent it on these matters which were unauthorized in so far as Parliament was concerned.
That runs clean contrary to the principle of parliamentary control of expenditures. If we are going to control them, then we have to review them first. That is why Estimates are normally tabled in March. This year we did not get them until May-or was it late April? If not that date, then it was the very last day of the sitting in April.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It was by House order.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis) says that it was by way of House order. That was the latest date that they could have been tabled. If there had been in place a good administration then those Estimates would have been forthcoming long before that day. They would have been tabled on the first day we were back, April 3. Instead, we waited, waited and waited to the end of the month to get the Estimates. We now have to consider these things while the money is being spent when normally consideration of those Estimates would be embarked upon prior to the expenditure of the money. There would have been a request for interim supply earlier and dealt with before the financial year began. We did not have that.
If Parliament is to retain control of the spending plans of the Government then, in my submission, we cannot have the money requested by Supplementary Estimates, have the House adjourn and have no dealings with those Estimates but simply dole out the money by the Government helping itself with special warrants.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: They want it both ways.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Hon. Member is absolutely right. The Government wants it both ways.
The second reason why I think there is doubt as to what the Government is doing is that the Financial Administration Act has never been used in this way before. This is a totally unprecedented method of using the Financial Administration Act, that is, to have the warrants signed and to dole the money out. It has never been done before.
Surely, if constitutional convention is to mean anything the practice established under constitutional principles must mean something. The practice in the country has been that these warrants are usable at certain times. Every other jurisdiction in the Commonwealth has got rid of these warrants. In every other jurisdiction the Government must turn to the Legislature to obtain approval for the money it will spend. However, in Canada we have stayed with this, if I may call it so, antiquated system for the convenience of the Government.
Convenience is one thing when Parliament is not around because it has been dissolved, or before it is recalled after an election. Once it has been recalled then, surely, the Government must consider the convenience of Parliament in deciding whether or not it should spend money and allow Parliament to make that decision.
What we have here is an abdication of the Government's responsibility to call this House back in good time and say: "We need your help. We need these expenditure plans approved. Thke your time, criticize them and make up your mind whether or not you want to allow it to happen. Give us the money". Instead, the Government had special warrants signed and said: "Now, approve all this afterwards". We are being asked to approve it in this Bill.
The third reason why I think the practice is irregular is that the Government itself has a special vote in the Estimates for contingencies. It has access to money voted by Parliament which it can use to tide itself over difficult moments when it runs short in one area and needs to apply additional funds. The vote is always granted by Parliament. There have been arguments about it but it always gets its way on this one. Treasury Board Vote 5 is named: "Government Contingencies".
May 15, 1989

In this year's Estimates $360 million were set aside for this little contingency item.
I would like to read what it says to describe this vote. This is the statement of authority that Parliament gives to the Government to use this $360 million. I would point out to Hon. Members just how vague it is. I am reading from the Main Estimates 1990-90:
-Subject to the approval of the Treasury Board, to supplement other votes for paylist and other requirements and to provide for miscellaneous minor and unforeseen expenses not otherwise provided for including awards under the Public Servants Inventions Act and authority to re-use any sums allotted for non-paylist requirements and repaid to this appropriation from other appropriations.
In other words, the money in this vote could have been used for the items contained in Supplementary Estimates B and then repaid when the Supplementary Estimates were approved. In fact, we know what happened. The Government spent the whole of the $360 million and then when it needed additional money it just had a warrant signed instead of coming to Parliament and asking for Supplementary Estimates B.
That is not a proper way to run the administration of the Government of Canada. The Government had a constitutional responsibility to come to Parliament and to ask for the money instead of proceeding with Governor General warrants.
Those are the three reasons why I believe there is doubt cast on the validity of the warrants. As long as the doubt exists, surely the amendment that has been proposed by the Senate which does not condemn the Government in any way clarifies that ambiguity and brings these warrants into their true light and indicates that they are not illegal, and that the next time this happens there may be another opinion. It leaves open the issue. It does not allow this to be a constitutional precedent which, in my submission, the passage of the Bill without the amendment will do. By rejecting this amendment it is saying: "Yes, we were right in bypassing Parliament in this way. Yes, it is fine for a Government to trample on the rights of Parliament and to ignore the essential right of Parliament to control the expenditure of money in this country".
That is not what the people of Canada want. It is not what we were elected here to do. That includes the Members of the Government on the other side.
There is another principle in our Constitution, that is, the principle that the sovereign is the fountainhead of all
Appropriation Act
justice. Indeed, in former times the Queen's or King's subjects could appeal to the monarch for relief from the problems that they were confronted with as a result of an unfair decision or harsh treatment by someone in authority over them. For that reason Members know that the King and the monarch in olden times established courts which could override manorial courts and lesser courts throughout the United Kingdom. We have transported that notion of the Crown's right to establish courts to this country. Now it is fettered, of course, by Parliament and the control that Parliament exerts over the Crown prerogative in that respect. It is similar to the process I described earlier.
One of the things that happens in this transfer is that the Crown exercises its prerogatives of mercy and of judicial control through a particular person, and that is the embodiment of all justice in this House, the Minister of Justice and the Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Lewis). Now, Mr. Speaker, one would have thought that someone in his position, the fountainhead of all justice on behalf of Her Majesty in Canada, would have acted in a judicial manner. Yet I have here an article that appeared in the Globe and Mail last Friday, and to say that I was shocked when I read this would be putting it mildly.
I would like to read what the Minister of Justice said, sir. These are not all his words but it will become obvious when it is. The learned writer, Mr. Windsor, of this column said:
The Government will not accept the Senate censure of some financial shortcuts it took when Parliament was recessed this winter, Conservative House Leader Doug Lewis told reporters yesterday.
I believe that is a reference to the Minister of Justice, Mr. Speaker.
He indicated that the Government will try to swing public opinion against the Upper House by mobilizing sympathy for war veterans whose pension cheques could be delayed next week because of the Senate move.
I will skip down another paragraph.
Veterans' regular pension cheques are due to be processed Tbesday and if the impasse is not sorted out by then, "We will give any veterans who call the phone number of Senator Allan MacEachen, the Liberal Leader in the Senate" Mr. Lewis added. The Government could get its spending Bill passed with simple resolution by the Commons concurring with the Senate's amendment. However, that would imply an acceptance of the Liberal criticism.

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
So Mr. Lewis told reporters the Government will be refusing the amendment and sending the Bill back to the Senate.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, does that sound like a Minister of Justice threatening the Senate, threatening these veterans with their pension cheques? Why would the Minister of Justice not say, "Well, the amendment that the Senate has proposed is fair and just, and so of course we will agree to it because we have the veterans' interests at heart."
Instead of that, he is trying to use the veterans as a whipping boy-

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: -to threaten the Senate, to threaten the other place. I say that it ill behooves the Minister of Justice to carry on in this way. He laughs, Mr. Speaker. All Hon. Members opposite seem to laugh when I talk about constitutional propriety. But they have an equal obligation with us on this side to uphold the Constitution of Canada, and I say that it is being breached in this case.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Now, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) made similar statements. Let me read from the same column:
The Liberal move was also criticized by Treasury Board President, Robert de Cotret. "They are arguing on a very minor procedural matter which should be debated in another forum", he said. "They are putting at risk a number of Government suppliers, Government employees and recipients of Government payments. That would be a very sad event should they not get them".
Mr. Speaker, here we have the same Minister this morning who made a statement and I would like to read from his statement, because he said in the newspaper column that this should be argued in another forum. I do not know why it would not be argued in the highest court in Canada, right here in Parliament, but he does not want to argue it here. He does not want to hear about it in this House. He does not want to hear about it in the other place. He wants to go by Governor General warrants. The only person he has to convince to sign those is Her Excellency and then he does not have to go outside the bounds of the Cabinet room. It can all be done secretly and hush-hush. He said in his statement
this morning, and I will quote him: "To accept the amendment is to imply that the Governor General acted contrary to law". So he said it was not illegal. He went on at some length to say it was not illegal. Why would he go and argue in another place if the Minister has this view? He is not inviting argument anywhere. He is saying he is right and that is all there is to it.
Why not accept the doubt and pass the amendment and get on with the matter instead of maintaining one position and stonewalling, and trying to make the Senate into a big bad wolf? Because that is exactly what the Government is doing. I suggest that the big bad wolf in this case is the President of the Treasury Board. I have some evidence that will back that up that I will give you in a moment, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to turn to the excellent work that has been done in the Senate and in the other place on this matter. This Bill was sent there and was referred by the Senate in its wisdom to its National Finance Committee which deliberated for some time and reviewed the provisions of this Act and the irresponsible way in which the Government had dealt with the control of the expenditures of this country. I would like to turn to the witness that the Senate Committee on National Finance called on Wednesday, May 10. They called someone who is an acknowledged constitutional expert in Canada. This person is not an expert who is acknowledged just as a Liberal expert by any means. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) refers to him at times as a constitutional expert. The Leader of the New Democratic Party has frequently referred to Senator Eugene Forsey as a constitutional expert. He was dragged out of retirement to speak on the subject of the outrage that had been committed by the Government in relation to its duty in dealing with financial matters in this House.
I would like to read some of his testimony before the Senate National Finance Committee.

When Parliament has been recalled and is there to vote supply, and when Supplementary Estimates have actually been presented, never

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT

He continued:
The House of Commons failed in its duty,-
Because the majority here, of course, stifled all opposition.
-just as it did shortly after the 1984 election on a subject of a borrowing bill. The Senate refused to pass the borrowing bill until the Estimates had been tabled. subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Oh, there is more, Mr. Speaker. There is more. Senator Frith on page 23 of the report asked the question of Dr. Forsey. He wanted to know what we-the Minister of Justice should control himself. Senator Frith said: "What can we do with this impropriety?"
What do you suggest we do? Is there any way open for us, other than refusing to pass the bill?
Dr. Forsey's answer was:
No, I do not think there is. I suppose that will make some people's hair stand on end, but I think that is the only way to stop it.
The next question, then, will be: What will follow that? Then I think the Government would have to draw up a new bill making whatever provision it considers necessary for the public service and including a retroactive clause dealing with this improper exercise of the use of Governor General's warrants. The wording would be "shall be deemed to have been" a legal action. That makes it retroactively legal but, as I
That is what Senator Forsey recommended. I suggest that what the Senate did was rather than defeat the Bill and cause a hubbub, it made a very small amendment incorporating the very amendment that this acknowledged constitutional expert suggested and put it in the Bill and sent it back to this House, and now the Government is saying: "Oh, no, we can't have that. It might imply criticism of our wrongful acts." If these acts were right the Government would have no worries about this anyway and it would let this amendment through, because on any reading there is no criticism of the Government in the wording of the amendment and that is perfectly clear.
Now I would like to turn to page 35 of the same evidence. Again we have some excellent words from Dr. Forsey on this matter. He said:
I do not think the question of whether it is a majority Government or a minority government is vital. I would agree that a minority government has more of an obligation to meet Parliament promptly than a majority government. I still think that Parliament ought to be summoned within a reasonable length of time, though I would agree that there is less pressure upon a majority government. The fact remains that this government did summon Parliament. As I understand it, it tabled some supplementary estimates when Parliament was sitting. It did not proceed with those estimates at all. It proceeded to do the things that have been described.
First, the government adjourned Parliament, and then it prorogued Parliament without making use of Parliament while it was there to be used. The government could have perfectly well dealt with this matter, and should have dealt with it according to proper usage.
He goes on:
The thing that is dangerous about this practice is, as Senator Stewart pointed out-and, if I remember correctly, was again pointed out by Senator Stollery-that if you accept this kind of action, then there is nothing to prevent a government from holding a one-day sitting, like Mr. Mackenzie King did in 1940, and then postponing the session. One day per year would be enough.
You say, "Oh, but no government would ever be unreasonable, no government would ever do anything wicked, no government would ever do anything improperly." I wish I had your faith. I remember what various people said and what I certainly said myself with great fervour when Mr. Mackenzie King dissolved Parliament after a one-day session in 1940. It was the most outrageous breach of proper constitutional practice. Heaven knows, I hold no brief for Mr. Mackenzie King. On the other hand, I have said on occasion that such and such a thing that would be dangerous to my mind is

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
perfectly constitutional. I am not concerned with who does it or what party is involved. I do not belong to any party now.
Those are the words of Dr. Forsey.
I have one more quote on page 37 of the same report, Mr. Speaker. Talking about the Government's actions in this matter, he said:
I think the practice is unreasonable, even though it was a relatively short delay, because of the precise circumstances which existed. That is the point. The danger is, as Senator Beaudoin has said, that you cannot fix an exact period, you cannot say two months, three months, four months or nine months. How many grains make a heap? At some point it becomes obviously improper. If you have the precedent of it being done for three months, then you can argue that you can do it for four months. If you can do it for four months you can say, "Well, it's been done for three months and now four months, so you can do it for five months."
Of course, all the way through you have the wonderful argument that it is absolutely legal and that can't be questioned except by a distinguished lawyer like, perhaps, Senator Frith or by an amateur, outsider, non-lawyer like myself. So you will have to have the argument made that it is perfectly legal, therefore everything is forgotten, forgiven, past.
That was the testimony the learned Senator gave before the Senate Committee on National Finance and I suggest that that evidence is cogent, it is reasonable, it is expert testimony and it deals with the issues at hand. The suggestion is very clearly made that this Government has failed to live up to its constitutional responsibilities. It has failed to deal with the business of supply in a reasonable way and it ought to have come to this House and had these estimates voted and approved at that time instead of using these special warrants in the way that it has.
I have another quote from the National Finance Committee. I must say this is a trifle embarrassing, I am sure, for the Government because it is the President of the Treasury Board giving his evidence as to what ought to be done in this case. He was being questioned by Senator Stewart on page 1:25 of the Proceedings of the Senate Committee on May 3, 1989. Senator Stewart asked the following question:
The mere fact that Parliament says you can find that there is an emergency does not mean in every circumstance that it is proper and legitimate to so do. I am not arguing at this point that what you have done is illegal.
I am saying that it is illegitimate under our Constitution. You have not been able to produce a single precedent to support your practice, but you have used Governor General's warrants in a case where a
Parliament has been called into session and the Parliament is adjourned-it is prorogued.
You have not produced a single example which supports your interpretation of this provision. I am spelling out to you what I think is a clear result that may follow from this. Of course, not under your Government but we may have a Mr. Trudeau again, or someone like that. Think what they will do, following your example. If your example is valid -
The Hon. Member laughs. He should listen to this, it is very important.
If your example is valid, do you dispute my assertion that it would then be possible for a government to finance itself the year out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund by Governor General's special warrants? Is there any reason on the supply side that it could not proceed in this way? You have your counsel with you. You know the Constitution and the law. What is the answer?
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) replied: "First of all if there were a government that had to sit as you say one day and immediately prorogue, then the law would entitle that Government probably to do it". That was the answer the Minister had. In other words, he is taking the view that Parliament could sit one day a year, be prorogued, and the Government could go on all year using special warrants, and help itself to the public funds of Canada. That is what the President of the Treasury Board thinks Section 30 of the Financial Administration Act means. Well, on a straight reading maybe, just maybe he is right. But maybe he is not. Let us assume for a moment he is right. What happens to our constitutional practice? What happens to the rights of Parliament? What happens to our control of government expenditures? It is out the window. We have no more control.
All the Members on the opposite side sitting behind the treasury benches will have no more say in what goes on in government matters because all the moneys will be expended by Governor General's special warrants if the Government chooses to do that. That is not the intention of the Constitution of Canada. That is not the intention of the Constitution Act, 1982. That is not the intention of the Financial Administration Act. So, the interpretation the Government is placing on this Act, in my submission, is doubtful at best. At worst, it is wrong and it should not be countenanced.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
That is the kind of answer the Government is giving, though. Mr. Speaker, let me continue with what the President of the Treasury Board said. Senator Stewart asked: "Do you think that would be legitimate and constitutional? That is an amazing interpretation, Mr. Minister". Mr. de Cotret answered: "I presume it would be legal". Senator Stewart asked: "But would it be legitimate? You are saying it would be legal."
May 15, 1989

Mr. de Cotret answers: "We are into a never-never land here". I will say we are. We should never be in this land. We should be dealing with this on a straight-up basis. Let us look at what is going on here. I would like to turn again to Section 30 of the Financial Administration Act. Section 30-1 have lost it. I should not have set it down.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I want to take this opportunity to thank my friend and give him an opportunity to find his notes.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis) is so helpful today. I wish he would agree to the amendment.
Section 30,1 could have done it off the top of my head, but I did not want to confuse the Minister by using words that were not exactly accurate. Section 30 starts off: "Where a payment is urgently required for the public good-". Now, that is the test. There must be urgency in the requirement for the payment. Yet what is the record of the Government in respect to this matter? Well, out of these special warrants it turns out from the operations of the committee in the other place, the Government managed to pay for the inspection of the shrubs at 24 Sussex Drive. This was $27,000 on a stupid expenditure. Now, the word "stupid" is not mine. That is the Prime Minister's word for describing that expenditure. The consideration of $27,000 for inspection of the shrubs to see what would best grow in the gardens of 24 Sussex Drive, which ones needed to be clipped, which ones needed to be trimmed, which ones needed to be pulled out by the roots, what new shrubs were needed to make the grounds look proper. A study worth $27,000-these
Appropriation Act
are not new shrubs, this was a study. This was a payment considered urgently required for the public good.
That was considered to be a payment urgently required for the public good, pursuant to section 30 of the Financial Administration Act. The money for that purpose was taken by special Governor General's warrants, and it cost $27,000 for a study of the shrubbery. I read in the newspaper this morning that Mr. Southam said that was not a bad deal because he had paid $10,000 for a similar study on his garden and his garden was much smaller than the garden at 24 Sussex Drive. He thought it was a bit of a bargain. The Prime Minister did not think it was a bargain. He thought it was stupid. Yet he and his Government have advised Her Excellency the Governor General to sign a special warrant stating that those funds were urgently required for the public good. It is a scandal.
There is much more. There is the case of the heralds at Rideau Hall, urgently required for the public good. We had to have heralds at once in order to give coats of arms to certain companies. Those hundreds of thousands of dollars were urgently required for the public good. That is what the Government meant when it had Her Excellency sign these warrants. It certified that the money was urgently required for the public good pursuant to section 30 of the Financial Administration Act, hauling out money to grant coats of arms to its wealthy friends.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: How much was that, $600,000?

speechtext:

That is not all. There has been the redecoration of Ministers' suites. We read just the other day how the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) was spending $35,000 soundproofing his office. It was a night to remember as Ambassador Derek Burney and his wife, Joan, entertained 560 guests at the official opening of the Canadian Embassy in Washington last week.

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
This must have been paid for out of special warrants as well.
And while Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and his wife, Mila, met such guests as Secretary of State James Baker and Senator Edward Kennedy on the sixth-floor balcony, embassy staff worked hard to make the event run smoothly. There was only one hitch: waiters had to substitute a French vintage for a missing shipment of Canadian wine. Still, embassy officials appeared to have chosen La Fleur brand wine with budgetary considerations in mind. For one thing, the French wines label-which waiters were careful to cover with linen napkins-proclaimed it to be "a premium wine at jug wine prices." A drink with a pleasing taste of fiscal restraint.
If Parliament had been in session, perhaps they could have gotten a better wine because we could have voted them the money, but this was spent under Governor General's special warrants. Perhaps that is why the Canadian shipment did not arrive. Perhaps the Government ran out of money and could not pay the Canadian shipper.
Having spent all this money on wine for the embassy opening, on heralds at Government House, on the study of the shrubbery at 24 Sussex Drive, we are told today that the Government will not have enough money after tonight to pay the veterans' pensions. The Government wasted the money. It used the money it took through Governor General's special warrants for all these crazy purposes it had in mind, authorized to itself under Supplementary Estimates B that were never approved in the House. Now the Government is saying that it does not have enough money left from what it took to pay the veterans their proper pensions. That is a disgraceful way to run the Government of Canada.
Canadians deserve better and this Government should live up to its responsibilities and see that the money is made available. It should have dealt with this matter back in March. Now it is rushing in here and telling us that the other place is holding this up by having passed an innocuous amendment that does not damage the Government's credibility or the substance of the Bill that has been passed.
There is no delay here on the part of the other place. The delay is at the behest of the Government. The Government House Leader himself told the newspapers on Friday that he was not having any of this amendment. All he has to do is say he agrees with it and we would have this amendment through the House today and it would receive Royal Assent tonight. Instead, the Government has brought in this motion to delay the matter further, to suggest that the other place has acted
improperly when in fact it has acted with great circumspection. It has dealt very favourably and positively with the legislation the Government has introduced. It has not suggested a change that damages the Government or alters the appropriation in any way, but one that corrects an apparent anomaly in the activities of the Government and its dealings with Parliament and the rights it may or may not have under section 30 of the Financial Administration Act.
It is very clear that section 30 of the Financial Administration Act requires that three tests be met before funds are transferred or appropriated by way of special warrant, and those three items are that there be an urgent requirement, that Parliament not be in session and that there be no other appropriation by which the payment could be made. The President of the Treasury Board has indicated his view that there was no other appropriation available, and I am inclined to believe him on that point because I think the Government had spent every cent it had and then some.
It is obvious it has to borrow money, and we will be dealing with that when we deal with the borrowing Bill, but it went ahead and borrowed money without the authority of Parliament but under the Financial Administration Act. It obviously had to borrow the money because it had over-spent what had been allocated to it. It introduced these Supplementary Estimates without having us consider them.
It is clear that there was no available way in which payments could be made. I will accept that. Parliament admittedly was not in session though it easily could have been. It is the Government's decision when to adjourn the House and when to call it back, and it was the Government's advice to Her Excellency to prorogue Parliament on February 28 that led to Parliament not sitting in March. It was the Government's advice to Her Excellency to summon Parliament on April 3, which meant that Parliament was not here to deal with this matter in a normal, expeditious manner in March.
