speechtext:
You should have listened to what I said. If you had, you would be agreeing with me. If you had any interest in defending the rights of this place and of your constituents, you would be on your feet saying the same things I am saying, instead of sitting there.
It is a shocking indictment of the Members on the other side that not one has risen to defend Parliament. They all agree with the President of the Treasury Board who has steamrollered this place and run over our rights. He says we have no right to question his judgment, that he acted in accordance with Section 30. If we do not have the right to question that judgment here, as I have said three times already, where do we have the right to question it? I do not have an obligation to go to the Supreme Court of Canada to decide whether the President of the Treasury Board has acted properly. That issue should be decided here, and Those Hon. Members at the back on the opposite side should be on their feet defending Parliament. They used to do it when they sat on this side of the House and when Liberal administrations sat there doing things like this, but they never did anything this bad. Now we are not hearing a peep.
This is an opportunity for Hon. Members to rise and say what they used to say in the past. I have forebome from quoting extensively from speeches made by old velcro lips, the former Hon. Member for Yukon, who used to speak about the rights of Parliament in the most heart-rending way. No one on the other side of the
Appropriation Act
House is following up on that kind of discourse. Where have those people gone?
What about Mr. Diefenbaker, who used to stand up for the rights of Parliament? He was a great Parliamentarian and acknowledged on all sides to be so. He fought for and defended the rights of this House. Why is no one rising, as he used to rise, to defend the rights of Parliament to deal with the most fundamental thing that we have to deal with under our Constitution, financial matters? Instead of that, there is dead silence. I say it is a shocking indictment of the Conservative Party and its change in priorities now that it has the responsibility of Government. It should learn to shoulder its responsibilities in accordance with the Constitution.
Their actions, in my submission, Mr. Speaker, under Section 30 of the Financial Administration Act, their dealings throughout the time we have been dealing with Bill C-14, with their method of tabling Estimates late, their failure to request supply in the Speech from the Throne, all of these indicate either a profound ignorance of the workings of the Constitution of Canada, which is shocking for a government, or a blatant disregard for their obligations pursuant to that Constitution to come to this place and present those spending proposals in a timely and sensible way so they can be dealt with in the normal way that Parliament deals with spending controls. It is our function and our responsibility that is being usurped by the Government using these special warrants. Instead of coming here and seeking authority, it goes to Her Excellency and says: "Sign on the dotted line and we will spend the money and thanks very much. We will get any authority we might need later."
In theory, and Senator Stewart and Dr. Forsey pointed it out in their evidence before the Senate committee, the Government could run with one day sitting per year for the next four years and ignore this House. Given the lack of initiative that this Government chose on any legislative matter, it could easily do just that. After all, think how they must have felt come February with those cold winds of February blowing. Boy, I can hear the Minister of Justice closeted with the President of the Treasury Board and the Deputy Prime Minister, saying: "We don't

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
want any criticisms in the House of Commons today. We don't want to read about our faux pas in the paper. We don't want to know about leaky budgets. We don't want to know about more possible resignations. We don't want to hear about any scandals.
So let's not have Parliament sit. Let us just govern by special warrant, and we will get all the money we need in special warrants and ignore Parliament because we don't want to have to put up with any embarrassing questions in Question Period. We don't want to have our spending plans reviewed by any committee. We don't want to have our spending plans discussed on the floor of the House where it might get some press attention." That is what is going on here. It is a cover-up operation and this Government has an obligation to come clean. I urge the Government to look at the words of the amendment. See how innocuous the amendment is. There is no criticism in the wording of the amendment of the Government's actions. I can safely say that had I been drafting the amendment it might have been a little stronger.
However, I am prepared to vote for the amendment even on the weakness that it contains; that is, it does not describe accurately in my view the improprieties that occurred. It legalizes whatever has happened, whether it was legal or illegal. I do not believe that in adopting the amendment the Senate has made any statement, that the matter is one way or the other. It has said there is doubt about the matter. To clarify the doubt, it has suggested this amendment to the legislation. I invite the Government to have another look at it, clarify the doubt, withdraw the motion that the President of the Treasury Board moved this morning and substitute another motion approving of the amendment, and let us get this Bill through and get the supply problem looked after. I do not want to see the President of the Treasury Board shedding more crocodile tears over the plight of the people that are not going to get paid. He knows how this can be done and it can be done very expeditiously with a little co-operation from the other side. I invite that co-operation.
We heard the Minister of Justice speaking some time ago about how important co-operation was. I recall the morning after the Budget leaked, he was in here talking about British parliamentary tradition and practice and how important co-operation was. I invite him to show that spirit of co-operation today, Mr. Speaker, and agree to the amendment. He has the power. He is the
Government House Leader. He can convince his colleagues that this amendment is satisfactory. He can get the President of the Treasury Board to withdraw this motion and substitute another that will adopt the amendment proposed in the other place. I invite him to do that, Sir, forthwith.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very rare that I would agree with something the Senate has done, but I must admit that this morning that we do agree despite the fact the Senate is not an elected place. What the Senate has done this morning in sending back this Bill to the House is slap the face of the Government. It has said to the Government: "You have done something that is wrong, something that is totally unconventional, something that is not very appropriate."
We have had the use of Governor General warrants four times in the last few months. Governor General warrants are usually used in very abnormal circumstances such as during a federal election campaign or perhaps when there is some other great emergency that prevents the Government from calling back Parliament to vote supply, to vote money for the ongoing expenses of this place. However, there are two things that really concern me about this Bill this morning presented by the government Minister. First, I think it is an affront to the supremacy of Parliament. This is the supreme institution of the land. The rights of Parliament, I believe, are being trampled upon. Second, I believe that the Government was afraid to meet Parliament back in January and February because of the economic activities and mergers that were going on in the country. This place could have been called back. This place should have been called back. In fact, March 6 was the agreed date to come back, but the Government was afraid to meet Parliament. It was afraid to meet this House. As a result, we now have the use of the Governor General warrant where billions of dollars was extended by it instead of being approved by Parliament.On January 19, the Governor General's warrant was used for the first time to spend some $80 million. On February 16, another $500 million was approved by a special warrant of the Governor General.
After the House was supposed to come back on March 6, and do not forget that Parliament was prorogued on February 28, instead of sticking to the original schedule and coming back on March 6 which had been agreed to, which we all expected, the Government was afraid to meet the opposition Parties in the House of Commons,
May 15, 1989

and on March 23 issued another Governor General warrant for $891 million.
On April 1, a Governor General warrant was issued for some $6 billion. That was on April Fool's day, two days before the House came back. My argument is that this is an abuse of Parliament. It is highly irregular, highly abnormal to use Governor General warrants in this way. My friends opposite of course are aware of that. The chairman of the Finance Committee is aware of that. He is aware of the conventional practice of Parliament. He is aware of the traditions of this place.
He is aware that the Governor General warrant is very seldom used except when an election is on or except when there is a legitimate excuse for Parliament not to be in session at that particular time. What happened here was very unconventional. What happened here is something that you very rarely see, very abnormal. I am concerned about the supremacy of Parliament. The most important thing about a Parliamentary system of democracy is that a Government has to come to the House and seek the approval of supply, to seek money to pay for the ongoing expense of government programs and government Departments. That is what responsible Government is all about. That is what the supremacy of Parliament is all about. I can imagine the speech that would have been made on this side of the House about 10,12 or 15 years ago by the former Prime Minister, John Diefenbaker.
He would have been making a speech about how the Government of the day was trampling on the rights of Parliament, how the executive had taken unto itself a tremendous amount of power to make decisions without consulting the people's representatives here in the House of Commons. I can remember Mr. Diefenbaker making speech after speech about Mr. Trudeau as Prime Minister ignoring the rights of Parliament and trampling upon the rights of this place and not consulting Parliament. I know the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis) can remember those speeches very well. If Mr. Diefenbaker were here, he would see this as one of the most momentous occasions this year as this Government tramples upon the rights of this place.
Not only Mr. Diefenbaker; two former House Leaders of the Conservative Party, Walter Baker and Jed Baldwin, made speeches about the rights of Parliament being trampled upon, about the precedents of Parliament
Appropriation Act
being changed, about conventions being changed by a Cabinet and by a Government across the way which in those days was of course a Liberal Government. The other point, Mr. Speaker, that really concerns me is the establishment of a very dangerous precedent by the Government. If we allow this to go on, if we allow this to proceed, then there is no saying that the Government next year will not do the same thing.
When the Government finds a certain amount of unpopularity over certain issues when Parliament is not in session, it will not recall Parliament. To carry on the expenditures of the Government, it will issue a Governor General warrant. If we let it go through this time, it will happen again, and again, and again. As a parliamentarian, that concerns me. It concerns me that we are abdicating much of our authority and power to the Prime Minister's Office and to Members of the Executive Council who sit across the way. This place will lose the purpose and the raison d'etre as to why Members were elected in the first place.
What we have seen in the last four months is without precedent. No Members on the government side can say that this was done in 1925, 1935, or in the 1940s, 1950s, 1960s, or 1970s. It is without precedent. That is why we have put forward this motion today. The motion sent here by the Senate states that the payments made by special warrants signed by the Governor General on January 19, February 16, March 23, and April 1, 1989 shall be deemed to have been legal. Of course, the Government disagrees with what the Senate has stated and the sending back of its motion.
One of the arguments I am making is what we are seeing here is the trampling of the rights of Parliament by a very arrogant Government. If Diefenbaker were present in the House, we would hear one of those splendid speeches about the rights of Parliament and the British tradition, and the Conservatives would be standing up and applauding him every minute of the way.
There is a second reason that this happened. It is not only an affront to the supremacy of Parliament, but the Conservative Party of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulro-ney) was afraid to meet Parliament in January, February, and March. The Government was afraid. It had rammed through the free trade Bill on New Year's eve, and it was afraid to do the correct thing and come back here in

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
January to get approval of government spending, government funds.
We all remember what happened in January. There were a lot of political issues in this country and the Government was on the wrong side. First, people were upset about the free trade deal and all the fallout from that deal.
Second, there was merger mania. Molson's Brewery merged with Carling O'Keefe. People were concerned about that. PWA, owned by Canadian Airlines, took over Wardair. People were also concerned about that and the concentration of power into fewer and fewer hands. I know the new Minister, the Member for Vancouver Centre (Ms. Campbell) must also be concerned about this.
There was the takeover of Imperial Oil by Texaco Canada. There was also the proposal from Stone Container of Chicago to take over Consolidated Bathurst. Bell Canada Enterprises took over Montreal Trustco. It was merger mania. We sent a letter to the Government House Leader and to the Speaker of the House suggesting that Parliament be recalled to deal with those matters, to have an investigation, and to debate those important issues in the House and with the people of Canada. The Government was afraid to meet the people on those issues, because it was on the side of merger mania and it knew that the people were not.
Not only did the Government not move the start of Parliament up to January or February, but it postponed the date of the commencement of Parliament from March 6 until April 3. The Government did that because it was afraid to meet the people of Canada here on the floor of the House of Commons.
It was not only merger mania, but there was the whole issue of American Express and turning it into a Schedule B bank. The bankers were concerned, and Canadians are concerned about the future of our country. Once again, the Government was on the wrong side of the issue. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was on the wrong side of the issue. I am sure even the chairman of the finance committee was afraid to face parliament on that particular issue. For that reason, the Government was afraid to call Parliament back. It was afraid to do the correct thing and recall the House of Commons to seek supply. It had to breach the rules of the House and the conventions, and the conventions of the Constitution of Canada and
seek a Governor General warrant to spend $7.5 billion of the people's money without a vote from the House of Commons.
Why else was the Government afraid to meet the House of Commons in February or even on March 6? It was afraid to meet the House of Commons because interest rates were rising and people across the country, including the small business community, farmers, workers, homeowners, and consumers were asking the Government why it did not stop this huge increase in interest rates. Parliament was crying to come back to deal with this important issue of high interest rates. Parliament was also crying to come back to talk to the Government about the deficit.
All of a sudden the Government discovered that the deficit was a big problem. It was not a problem during the election campaign, but it was a problem in the new year of 1989. The Government needed an extra month to run around slashing and cutting the budgets of various Departments which affected ordinary people, such as child care, farm programs, and unemployment insurance. The Government did not want Parliament here interfering by asking legitimate questions on behalf of ordinary Canadians. That is why we did not come back. That is why on April Fools' Day the Government had a Governor General warrant signed for $6 billion. When the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) testified before the Senate he stated that that was a rather large amount, it was abnormal, and that it had not happened before. When he was asked for a precedent, he could not provide any type of precedent, because it had not happened before.
For expedient political purposes and for narrow partisan purposes Parliament was not recalled. The Government, acting as a republican government like that of the United States of America, with the Prime Minister's Office and the Privy Council's Office, decided to seek more than $7 billion of money with a Governor General warrant.
If we allow the Government to get away with this, who is to say that when we recess in the summertime, or if there is an unpopular issue next fall that Parliament will not return in September, but perhaps will not return until late in October or November. Once again the Government will use the method under Governor General warrant to pay the pensioners, the veterans, and to
May 15, 1989

continue improving the garden at 24 Sussex, or making a closet larger for the Gucci shoes of the Prime Minister.
For narrow, partisan political purposes the Government was afraid to meet the people of Canada here on the floor of the House of Commons. For those reasons, I want to move an amendment to the motion that is before the House. The amendment is seconded by my House Leader, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). It states:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after 'April 1, 1989" and substituting with "may respect the letter of the law, but are unconventional and set a dangerous precedent".
We are moving that amendment because the Government may argue that the letter of the law has not been broken. I notice that Eugene Forsey in the Senate has stated that, in his opinion, it is not constitutional. It is certainly not conventional. It is setting a very dangerous precedent.
I say to Members opposite that they will be here forever. If this type of dangerous precedent is set in terms of parliamentary democracy, even if the present Government does not use it again in this session of Parliament, what will prevent a future Government in 10 or 20 years from saying back in 1989 a Conservative Government used a Governor General warrant four times when it could not recall Parliament. It does set a very dangerous precedent. All the testimony to the Finance Committee in the Senate told us that it was indeed very unconventional.
I wish to make one final appeal to Members opposite to think back to the history and tradition of their party. Year after year the Conservative Party used to argue on the floor of the House of Commons about the supremacy of Parliament, about how more power and authority was taken away from Parliament into the Prime Minister's Office. It was taken away from Parliament and given to the Cabinet. It was taken away from Parliament and given to the bureaucracy, Departments, and Deputy Ministers and all the bureaucrats. We heard speech after speech about the supremacy of this place and how important it was that we make decisions about supply. There is no more important issue than voting on the use of the people's money. The money does not belong to
Appropriation Act
the Conservative Party of Canada or the Prime Minister. It belongs to the taxpayers.
The Government did not come to Parliament to seek approval for that supply. It did not come to Parliament to seek approval for the appropriation of more money for the Prime Minister's garden, for his closet, for pension cheques or anything else. That sets a dangerous precedent.
I appeal to the best traditions of the Conservative Party to consider our amendment and support it. If it is not supported I believe the Government runs the risk of establishing a precedent that could be very dangerous in the years ahead.
I know that the chairman of the Finance Committee agrees with me. He is an honest and forthright person. He knows the history of this place and the history of his Party. He knows that what happened was irregular and unconventional.
The Minister of Justice knows that as well. He knows what kind of speech he would have made if Pierre Trudeau had done this. He would be moving this kind of amendment and expressing concerns about the blatant disregard of Parliament.
The Minister of Justice knows that his Government was afraid to call Parliament back last February and March. Our House Leader sent him a letter on two or three occasions, requesting that the Government to recall Parliament to discuss the American Express issue, to deal with the question of mergers. He received similar letters from the Liberal Party.
He knows that Canadians wanted Parliament to come back. He knew that the fiscal year would end on March 31 and any money the Government needed should be approved by Parliament. He knew the Government would have to ask the Governor General to sign a warrant for $800 million and another for $6 billion on April 1.
While Parliament could have been called back, the Conservatives were afraid to do so. They were afraid to meet the people of Canada. It was preparing a Budget that would cut and slash day care programs, unemployment insurance programs and programs for ordinary

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
people. It was in the process of jacking up interest rates and jacking up the unemployment rate in this country. That is why Parliament was not called back.
In conclusion, I appeal to my friends in the Conservative Party to get up and speak their mind. Let them remember the traditions of their Party. Let them remember the speeches they made on this side of the House when they talked about the supremacy of Parliament, about political expediency. Then they will vote with us in support of this amendment before the House today.

speechtext:
The Chair finds the amendment to be in order. Questions or comments.
My question is based on this interview of Mr. Chadder-ton. The question was: "Is that what you think of this whole kerfuffle? That people are being disregarded in this power struggle?" Mr. Chadderton said:
Yes, its very clear to me, and I have been around Ottawa a long time, that the Government was wrong. They tried to put these money Bills through. When the Senate got back into action, the Senate said: "Look, we have the authority" and they sent the Bills back. It is a question of whose right or wrong and of course the Senate, whether we agree with it or not, is doing what it can do. So the Government does not really want to knuckle under to the Senate. And then we see a big play by Doug Lewis, the Government House Leader, who says: "Well of course we are going to try to line up public support by telling them that the pensioners are going to go without their cheques". You know, if this was a major issue I would not think this way but it is not a major issue, it is a little territorial dispute between the Commons and the Senate.
The interviewer then asked:
Well, if that is the case, shouldn't the Senate forget about the amendment and say alright, it is importantthat the veterans gettheir cheques and other people, employees of the Government, civil servants and let us just accept this as it is?
Mr. Chadderton answered:
I would say that until someone decides to abolish the Senate you have to look at constitutionally who is right and who is wrong. And the Senate is doing what it has the power to do. Second, from my
reading it is a fairly simple matter for the Government to go back, rework the money Bill and send it back to the Senate.
So on one hand perhaps we should say: "Yes we will go along with applying pressure to the Senate". I don't think veterans are going to think that way because they know as I know, that the Senate has the power to do what it is doing.
These people have fought for Parliamentary democracy once. I suggest that the interview indicates that they are quite prepared to do it again. The Government should respect the rules of parliamentary democracy.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO.l, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree. The Government's action is an abuse of the rights of Parliament. It is an abuse of the supremacy of Parliament. If we allow the Government to proceed it will set a dangerous precedent.
We are not talking about a few dollars, we are discussing a Governor General warrant for $6 billion on April 1. This legislation concerns another Governor General warrant for $891 million for March.
Parliament was supposed to return on March 6. It did not come back because the Government was afraid to meet the people of Canada. Instead, it had two Governor General warrants signed for some $7 billion. That has not been done before. We were not at war. The Government could have recalled the House and we could have examined the Supply Bill. Parliament could have passed judgment as to whether it wanted to appropriate this $7 billion for the Government to fulfil its obligations during that period. But it chose not to come back.
If we allow this arrogant Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis) and the Conservative Party to do this now, it will

happen again. Parliament will be giving greater power to the executive, to the Cabinet and the Prime Minister's Office. This is not a republican system of Government. We are not in the United States.

This is not France with a republican system of government. In Canada, it is different. We have a parliamentary system here.

The most important principle in a parliamentaiy system of government is for the Government to come to Parliament and ask for spending approval.
I know some veteran Members on the other side, like my friend, the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kem-pling), know that that is true. He is dying to get up and make a speech about how the Government and the Prime Minister are trampling on the rights and traditions of this place. That is precisely what is happening. They are doing it for narrow partisan purposes. They want to prevent us from asking questions about interest rates, mergers, child care or unemployment insurance, or the fact that drought payments have not gone to western Canadian farmers. That is why Parliament was not recalled.
In the meantime the Government was planning a vicious Budget in an assault on ordinary Canadians. It did not want us to ask questions about it. It wants to control the political agenda and news agenda just like the President in the United States and the President in France.
It is time that the Government back-benchers display some courage and independence. It is time they spoke their minds and read the speeches they made, that Diefenbaker made, that Walter Baker and Jed Baldwin made year after year about the supremacy of this place.
Now that the Conservatives are in Government they are opportunists. It is no wonder that people are cynical. It is no wonder that at the next election they will finish third.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: PEACE PLAN FOR WEST BANK AND GAZA STRIP-NEGOTIATION OF PALESTINIAN SELF-RULE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to read that Israeli Prime Minister Yitzak Shamir's plan for peace was approved by his Cabinet with a 20 to 6 margin.
The plan calls for "free, democratic and secret" elections of leaders in the West Bank and Gaza Strip to negotiate Palestinian self-rule in the territories. The first phase of this plan would have the Palestinians ruling autonomously under the aegis of Israeli military forces for at least three years before talks take place to resolve permanently the status of the occupied lands.
This plan was presented to President Bush in the U.S. six weeks ago. There have already been negative comments from several sources. However, Bethlehem Mayor Elias Freij told Israel's Arabic TV that the plan is a "worthy idea if it is fairly conducted under international supervision with the consent of the PLO and the participation of the residents of East Jerusalem".
I know Canada would be more than willing to assist with any international supervisory process. Let us hope that this latest plan will be a significant step forward to a real and enduring peace.

subtopic: HARSHEST EFFECT ON WOMEN
HARSHEST EFFECT ON WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a northern Canadian, as a native person and as a female, I represent people who have been affected by the Government's Budget beyond anything which could possibly resemble fairness, justice and equality. The poorest of Canada's poor are unquestionably women. The Government obviously finds that satisfactory.

May 15, 1989
The Budget continues its punishment, particularly of native people, women and of children, not only in Canada. Now the Government has hit hard the most impoverished people in the world.
Some 50 per cent of all women-led families live well below the poverty line, as do more than four out of every ten single women, most of whom are widows over the age of 65. One in every five Canadian children is being raised in poverty. One in every eight Canadian women is a battered woman.
The Government could not see fit to be sufficiently courageous and caring about these Canadians without spreading its greed even further to the women of the developing world.
I am saddened and ashamed that the Government through its Budget has reinforced the fact that in spite of great wealth and privilege for some, there is a growing under-class of Canadians in which by far the greatest number of disadvantaged are women and their children.

subtopic: HIGH COST OF HOUSING-HARSH EFFECT ON WOMEN
HIGH COST OF HOUSING-HARSH EFFECT ON WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently, the Minister of State for Housing (Mr. Redway) admitted publicly that the Government has not been doing a good job on housing. He invited Canadians to give him a blast.
I would like to draw to his attention two groups of Canadians who are unable to do this because they are fully preoccupied making ends meet. Some 60 per cent of single parent families headed by women and 50 per cent of single elderly women have an income below the poverty line.
The Government's callous budget policies of high interest rates, the gutting of social housing programs and now the imposition of a goods and service tax on housing means a larger number of women are being driven into poverty because of the high cost of housing.
I call upon the Government to reverse its policies so that all women in Canada are able to afford adequate housing. In particular, I call for the full funding of the
co-operative housing program and the reinstatement of the RAAP.
Surely, the Government must consider the needs of these women for shelter, not just the needs of those wealthy people living on Sussex Drive.

subtopic: TOURISM IN RESSOURCE REGIONS OF QUEBEC
TOURISM IN RESSOURCE REGIONS OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Andre) has announced that the tourism aspect of the business development program in Quebec's resource regions, Gaspe-Magdalen Islands, Lower St. Lawrence, North Shore, Saguenay-Lake St. John, Charlevoix, Northwestern and Northern Quebec, will take effect immediately.
Mr. Speaker, with this program in effect, the resource regions have an action strategy that will enable the tourism industry in each of these regions to participate fully in economic development.

subtopic: CLOSURE OF CFB PORTAGE
CLOSURE OF CFB PORTAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the weekend I joined the people of Portage la Prairie in protest over the proposed closure of CFB Portage. While hundreds of local people attended the rally, notable by their absence were the local Member of Parliament, the senior Minister for Manitoba, and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. McKnight). It is clear that the Minister of National Defence does not have the courage to come to my home province and face the people there who have been singled out for over one-third of the personnel cuts now proposed for the military.
The effect of the closure on CFB Portage, combined with the cut-backs to Kapyong Barracks in Winnipeg, will have a devastating impact on Manitoba. The closure of CFB Portage alone will result in the loss of some 580 military personnel, 180 civilians, and will pull $20 million directly out of the local economy.
May 15, 1989

At the same time, Defence Department spending will increase in Alberta, home of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), and in Saskatchewan, home of the Minister of National Defence.
Manitoba is expected to shoulder the burden of deficit reduction. The people of Manitoba ask only for fairness. Why can this Government not be bothered to listen?

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO SWIFT CURRENT BRONCOS-MEMORIAL CUP WINNERS
TRIBUTE TO SWIFT CURRENT BRONCOS-MEMORIAL CUP WINNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to report on one of the most remarkable stories in the annals of hockey.
Two winters ago I rose in this House to report on a tragic bus accident which claimed the lives of four members of the Swift Current Broncos Junior Hockey Team. Today, on a much happier note, I pay tribute to the Swift Currrent Broncos, a team imbued with indomitable prairie spirit, a team which picked itself up out of the wreckage of that accident and which, on Saturday, attained the pinnacle of Canadian major junior hockey league supremacy by winning the Memorial Cup.
I want to congratulate Coach Graham James, Bronco President John Rittinger, the players and the entire community of Swift Current and southwestern Saskatchewan, a community which has so solidly supported the team through thick and thin.
I know that all Members of the House will want to join with me in congratulating the Swift Current Broncos.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO SWIFT CURRENT BRONCOS-MEMORIAL CUP WINNERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
subtopic: EFFECT OF GLOBAL ECONOMY ON WOMEN

maintopic: NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
subtopic: EFFECT OF GLOBAL ECONOMY ON WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Rosamaria Ruiz, a journalist and community health worker from Bolivia, addressed several hundred women at the annual general meeting of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. Her presentation was a sobering assessment of the present state of the global economy, and was a call for solidarity among
women who are the hardest hit by economic recessions, poverty and war.
It is sad that at a time when Canada could be taking a leading role in the movement for international peace and justice, the Conservative Government is taking the opposite direction by reducing Canada's aid to countries in need. Countries in the Third World are faced with crippling foreign debt. It is from their experience that we must learn about dealing with our own.
Canada must not withdraw from the problems of international development but, rather, should be seeking, in co-operation with poorer countries, new and creative ways to achieve prosperity and justice for all.

subtopic: APPROPRIATENESS OF BAN ON BEN JOHNSON
APPROPRIATENESS OF BAN ON BEN JOHNSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 26, 1988, the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Charest) purported to ban, for life, a constituent of mine, Mr. Ben Johnson, from participating on Canadian national teams. He did this without providing any form of hearing to Mr. Johnson. To accomplish this, the vehicle he used was the media.
Given that the Fitness and Amateur Sport Act provides funding mechanisms only, where does the Minister get his authority to ban anyone from competing? The enabling statute makes no provision for banning anyone from sports competition.
If the Minister had read Section 2 of the Fitness and Amateur Sport Act, he would have realized that the Minister responsible for that Act is the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty) and not himself.
This Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport, full of self-importance, announced to the world that he was going to ban my constituent from competing in Canada when no Minister is empowered to do such a thing and when, incredibly, he legally is not even the Minister responsible for his own statute.
This is another example of the arrogance of the Conservative Government and an example of its lack of respect for the liberties of the individual.

May 15, 1989

subtopic: CONSTITUENT CONTRIBUTES $100
CONSTITUENT CONTRIBUTES $100
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the House the patriotic actions of a constituent of mine.
This Saturday I held a town hall meeting in the Windsor Park Community League Building to discuss the Budget, the annual deficit and the national debt. At that meeting Mrs. Rita Bustin, a kindergarten school teacher and single parent, presented me with a cheque for $100 made payable to the Government of Canada. Mrs. Bustin gave me this money to put toward the national debt, not the interest but the principal. I applaud Mrs. Bustin and other Canadians like her who are so concerned about the debt and want to do something about it.
Thus, to the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the best Finance Minister this country has ever had, I stand in this House to offer the $100 cheque Mrs. Bustin gave to me this weekend.

subtopic: WOMEN'S CHOICE IN REPRODUCTION
WOMEN'S CHOICE IN REPRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a humane society does not want to go back to a time when women were criminals for exercising their right to reproductive choice. Reproductive choice is a basic human right.
We must keep this right, we must ensure that abortion is in no case again considered a criminal act by restoring funding for family planning, by conducting more research to develop safe, effective contraceptives and finally, by ensuring that all women in Canada have equal access to reproductive health services.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT PLANNING
EMPLOYMENT PLANNING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, people sometimes wonder about the purpose of
our job strategy programs. Under the previous government, they only generated temporary jobs without prospects for the future. Today, these programs are meant to give workers an opportunity to get into or get back into the labour market.
In a press release issued last week, an organization in my riding called "La traversee intemationale du lac Memphremagog'' said, and I quote: "The training and job experience La traversee intemationale gave these workers and students helped them acquire new skills, make contacts within the job environment and adjust to that environment."
Mr. Speaker, a follow-up of the twelve employees revealed some very positive results: one permanent job with La traversee intemationale; one permanent job in the private sector; three full-time jobs in the private and community sectors; two part-time jobs in the private and community sectors; one start-up of a private business and four returns to full-time studies.
Mr. Speaker, that is good news for the people in the Magog area and my riding.

subtopic: THUNDER BAY FLYERS WIN CENTENNIAL CUP JUNIOR A CHAMPIONSHIP-THUNDER BAY TWINS WIN ALLAN CUP SENIOR CHAMPIONSHIP FOR FIFTH TIME
THUNDER BAY FLYERS WIN CENTENNIAL CUP JUNIOR A CHAMPIONSHIP-THUNDER BAY TWINS WIN ALLAN CUP SENIOR CHAMPIONSHIP FOR FIFTH TIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two Canadian sporting events took place last weekend that affected the City of Thunder Bay. I am pleased to report to this House that on Saturday, the Thunder Bay Flyers hockey team beat Prince Edward Island to win the Centennial Cup Junior "A" Hockey Championship. This is the first time that this cup has come to Thunder Bay.
Also, this past week the Thunder Bay Twins hockey team won their fifth Allan Cup Senior Hockey Championship. This sets a Canadian record for the number of Allan cups won by the Thunder Bay Twins. The efforts of the Flyers' coach, Dave Siciliano, and the Twins' coach, Bill MacDonald, and the outstanding performance of all the hockey players should be commended.
May 15, 1989

Thunder Bay and northern Ontario are convincingly emerging as the hub of amateur hockey in Canada, proving once again that rural and small town Canada does produce winners.

subtopic: DEVASTATION CAUSED BY FOREST FIRES
DEVASTATION CAUSED BY FOREST FIRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are now more than 100 forest fires burning in Manitoba. One of the worst is in my riding in western Manitoba. It started Thursday and as of one hour ago now encompasses 120,000 acres.
The communities of Cowan, Briggs Spur, and Renwer have been evacuated. The main highway, No. 10, has been closed. A state of emergency is in effect for the Minitonas and Mountain area. All access to the Duck and Porcupine Mountains has been closed.
The dedicated people working for the Manitoba Department of Natural Resources are doing a superhuman job in handling the logistics of battling such a destructive fire. Also involved are 120 firefighters, 21 cats, 12 skidders, 7 helicopters, and 4 water bombers.
The current situation is described as stable but extremely volatile due to near 30 degree Centigrade heat and variable winds. What is needed now more than anything else is rain.
* # *

subtopic: FEDERAL SUBSIDIES TO FOSSIL FUEL MEGA PROJECTS
FEDERAL SUBSIDIES TO FOSSIL FUEL MEGA PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians who care about the global environment are wondering why the Budget overlooked $5 billion in federal subsidies to fossil fuel mega projects.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp) says the energy mega projects represent the country's best strategy to remain self sufficient. The Minister is wrong on two counts. The International Energy Agency informs us we are using inefficiently 30 per cent of our energy. Therefore, if we learn to use energy efficiently we would rediscover an extra 30 per cent of energy we presently waste.
Second, we have a responsibility in reducing the trend in global warming. The mega projects would consider-
Oral Questions
ably increase carbon dioxide pollution in Canada at a time when the world is looking for ways of cutting such pollution.
Why does the Minister of Energy ignore the environment while the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) proclaims his commitment to sustainable development?

subtopic: CONCERNS EXPRESSED ABOUT SOCIAL PROGRAMS AT WEEKEND MEETING
CONCERNS EXPRESSED ABOUT SOCIAL PROGRAMS AT WEEKEND MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the weekend hundreds of women came from across Canada to meet in Ottawa to discuss issues not only of importance to women but to Canadians generally. Amongst the issues that they discussed were concerns about child care, about native rights, about pensions, about issues affecting the disabled, in fact, issues concerning all Canadians.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, this morning when these hundreds of women stayed over to talk to politicians who have it in their power to do something to address those concerns, the Government decided not to show up.

speechtext: Shame, shame.

subtopic: CONCERNS EXPRESSED ABOUT SOCIAL PROGRAMS AT WEEKEND MEETING
speechtext: I do not think that is at all acceptable, either to the women of Canada or to Canadians generally.

subtopic: CONCERNS EXPRESSED ABOUT SOCIAL PROGRAMS AT WEEKEND MEETING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
My question is for the Minister of Finance and it concerns the closures and reductions at Armed Forces bases as a result of his Budget. He should know by now that western Prince Edward Island has been devastated by the closing of Summerside, and that 40 per cent of the

May 15, 1989
Oral Questions
military cuts contemplated by the Budget fall on the people of Manitoba.
I would like to refer him to a situation in New Brunswick. I would like to quote a press release of April 21, 1988, which states:
The Minister of National Defence, the Honourable Perrin Beatty, announced today plans to keep Canadian Forces Base, (CFB) Chatham, N.B., as a viable, operating base.
'I am pleased to reassure the community of Chatham that our commitments will not only be kept, but enhanced,' said Mr. Beatty. This activity will ensure that the Chatham airfield remains fully operational well into the 1990's.
That is the end of the quote, Mr. Speaker. In an attempt to win seats in the last federal election in New Brunswick, the Minister of National Defence of the day went out of his way to assure the people of Chatham and the people of New Brunswick, by way of a special announcement, that the CFB base at Chatham, New Brunswick, would be increased in size and remain fully operational.
How does the Government now justify violating the promise to the people of New Brunswick? How does the Government now justify slashing the operations of the CFB base at Chatham?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
I would like to say to the Minister, if the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister are not intervening, it is both offensive to the people of Canada and dangerous that this Government has adopted a defence policy in scrapping its 1987 White Paper on Defence, not based on military priorities or based on our commitments to our allies, but on purely partisan politics.
That fact is, the closures or reductions announced by the Minister of Finance at Canadian Forces bases in Summerside, Gander, Sydney, Moncton, Chatham, Ottawa, North Bay, London and Winnipeg all have one thing in common; they are in ridings held by Liberal Members of Parliament. Nine of the fourteen base reductions in this country are in ridings held by the Liberal Party. Are we supposed to believe that this is a coincidence, Mr. Speaker? speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister who just spoke about years of inaction in child care. Her Government has added years of inaction to years of inaction in child care. That is all.

The Catholic Women's League met with individual Ministers at great length. I have met with the
