speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I an pleased to have an opportunity once again to speak on this issue which I brought to the attention of the House sometime ago. You will recall that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Mr. Milliken), and I rose in the House on Thursday, April 6, 1989 to make the House aware of the grievance we had concerning the use of a Governor General special warrant by the Government.
When we are discussing Governor General special warrants we should not confuse them with Governor General warrants of the kind that have been used on a relatively regular basis by the Government in order to
Appropriation Act
administer the affairs of the nation. Today we are talking about the use of an instrument granted to the Government by virtue of the Financial Administration Act under a section that has been used improperly. We made that case in the House on April 6, and then the Bill in question was passed shortly afterward.
The Estimates were tabled in the House on April 28. The House adopted, albeit reluctantly, the interim supply requested by the Government, and the Bill went to the other place. Many of the points that my colleague from Kingston and the Islands raised in terms of our grievance with the Government's use of these so-called special warrants were indeed taken up again in the Senate Banking Committee.
I was there last week, where I heard witnesses like Dr. Eugene Forsey and others inform the committee of the other place how inappropriate and unprecedented were the use of these special warrants. Clearly the Government has put itself in a veiy difficult situation. In my opinion not only have the rules of the House been abused, certainly the spirit if not the text of our Constitution has been abused as well. The Financial Administration Act has been bent out of shape in a serious way by the Conservative Government. The Senate recognized this in its deliberations.
Ultimately we have to grant supply to the Government in order for it to operate. At the same time I cannot as a Member of Parliament accept what the Government has done. It has breached those privileges which I feel I have in the broad sense, recognizing that Mr. Speaker has indicated that in terms of the orders of this House there has not been a prima facie case.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that if we get into the broad sense of the definition of privilege, and in particular if we take into consideration the fact that our privilege and how we operate in this House are granted by virtue of a section of our Constitution, which section states that we operate in a manner similar to that of the Mother of Parliaments, I feel that we have definitely been offended.
Even if no privilege of a Member has been breached in the narrow sense of our definition of privilege, or in the broader sense, Mr. Speaker made it very clear a few days ago in his deliberation on our questions of privilege that in fact he was not ruling on whether or not the Bill was

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
legal. I wish to refer to the ruling given by the Chair, as reported at page 1178 of Hansard of May 2, 1989:
The question of whether or not the terms of the Financial Administration Act have been respected in this instance is not a matter that was raised in the arguments put forward on April 6, nor indeed is it a matter upon which the Chair would be in a position to rule.
The Chair has stated that it is not in a position to rule on the legality of the way that the Financial Administration Act is applied in this particular case.
The Chair stated further:
The Chair has no authority to venture beyond the realm of parliamentary practice and procedure into questions of law.
I believe if we go a little further in the decision of Mr. Speaker of that day we will see that he also tells us that, indeed, he has no authority to determine whether or not our Constitution has been respected in this case. What do we have now? We have a situation in which I as an opposition Member and everyone else recognize that the Government needs funds in order to operate. However, at the same time we cannot accept what has been done. We cannot recognize that as being a valid precedent for the future. I will get into why we cannot do that in a few moments.
However, before I do that, I want to express the solution that was offered to us by the Senate. The Senate has sent to us a message in which it has recommended the following change: "The payments made by special warrant signed by the Governor General on January 19, February 16, March 23, and April 1, shall be deemed to have been legal". If I had my way I would add another sentence to that which would state: "They shall be deemed to have been legal but shall not constitute any precedent that could be applicable again". I would do that in order to ensure that the Government does not feel it has the right in the future to do what it has done before.
My colleagues to my left have proposed an amendment to the motion offered by the Government. First, the Government has responded to the amendment from the Senate by stating that it feels that the Bill is already legal. To this some of our colleagues have proposed an amendment which would add the words: "that the Bill may respect the letter of the law but are unconventional and set a dangerous precedent". Of course, that is quite true. The amendment is quite definitely supportable. I
would like to support it. I know that other of my colleagues would do so as well. However, it even goes further than what was stated in the amendment from the New Democratic Party.
A few moments ago I was describing to you, Mr. Speaker, why this is a dangerous precedent and why we cannot recognize what has happened here as being acceptable.

First all, Mr. Speaker, the Governor General's special warrants are usually granted by Her Excellency when the Government so requests, at times when it is impossible for Parliament to decide whether or not to approve the Government's appropriations.
Mr. Speaker, of course the only time when it is not possible for Parliament to approve appropriations is during an election campaign. Before the turn of the Century, there may have been times when a session lasted only two months of the year, and six or seven months later, when the Government needed funds to repair the roof of the Parliament Buildings, it was not going to recall the House just for that. In that case, the Government could ask the Governor General for these appropriations, which would be approved by the House retroactively. That is why the House added to the Financial Administration Act a section that deals with exceptional situations.
Briefly, Mr. Speaker, Parliament must not be in session and there must be a specific or special situation. In fact, the warrants are called Governor General's special warrants. And of course, there must be no other way to obtain the funds. As far as that goes, this Government had more or less made sure there was no other way. The Government intentionally adjourned the House without giving Parliament a chance to approve appropriations.
Why did the Government do this? I hope they will be able to answer this question later on, because so far, Mr. Speaker, their answers have not been very convincing.
So first, the Government may have been unable to do otherwise, but the situation was of its own making.
Second, the Government says there was a so-called urgent need and that the House was not in session. May I remind you once again that the reason you were not in


;

:

session was the result of a deliberate act on the part of the Government opposite?

When we talk about the test of whether or not the section of the Financial Administration Act can be used, it is important to note a few things. First, Parliament was recalled last year on December 12. It is quite evident to me that if the Government required supply to cover the duration of the election campaign and a normal postelectoral period which it took to recall Parliament and, perhaps, a few days into the new session, the House should recognize that there is nothing precedent setting here and that in fact we must give the Government those funds.
However, that is not the point. Parliament was recalled. Parliament sat. Parliament listened to the Throne Speech. Then Parliament voted on the Throne Speech. Parliament voted on a Bill, the free trade Bill. Once that Bill had been passed the Government did not seek supply. The Government adjourned Parliament. The Government caused the adjournment of Parliament. Once that was done we were in recess for some weeks.
When the Government had used up all its money under Vote 5 of the Treasury Board, which it can seek when the House is not sitting, it then decided to seek a Governor General special warrant. This is something rather unprecedented because Parliament had sat.
However, if that were not bad enough, once it sought those first one or two Governor General warrants pending the recall of Parliament in the same session-we were not prorogued, we were only in recess-lo and behold what did we have? We had the Government not recalling Parliament the way it said it would, but instead it prorogued Parliament in the month of April, deliberately causing itself, if you wish, Mr. Speaker, to go broke, causing itself to be in a situation in which it would be out of funds, not temporarily, but to the end of the fiscal year and for a portion of the next year.
To remedy the mess that it had created for itself the Government introduced Bill C-14 in this House, which apart from everything else will be the only appropriation Bill passed by this Parliament in a year and a half.
Appropriation Act
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Timer) said very eloquently in the past when we were discussing the the budget leak how important it was for the House of Commons to have the authority to decide what grievance it wanted to air with Parliament and what issue it wanted to bring to Parliament before it granted supply to the Government. This is not just an archaic tradition. Surely this House, a House of Members elected by the people of Canada, has the right to decide what issues to bring forward to the attention of the Government. To decide if we wanted to grant or to deny supply to this Government is not just a tradition.
Democracy is not just something that should be fondly remembered. It should be applied. It is the Government's role to ensure that the privileges of Members and the democracy in which we live is respected. It must ensure that as Members of Parliament we get to decide what funds are spent by the Government.
They should not create a situation where they ask the Governor General for special warrants, where they recall Parliament and fail to ask for supply, where they cause a recess, where they cause a prorogation of Parliament, where they recall it later and say: "Guess what, House of Commons, we forgot to ask you for some money a year ago. We have been broke ever since. We have asked the Governor General to give us money meanwhile, and now we want you to ratify all this, and do not complain."
That is what the Government has told this House. That is not right. The least we can do to rectify the damage done to this country and to this Parliament by the Government is to adopt the motion brought to our attention by the other place. If we do not do that, we should support the amendment offered to the House today and at the very least not recognize what the Government has done as being right. Perhaps we have no choice now but to give money to the Government across the way to administer the affairs of the nation, but we must insert it in the Bill or in a motion that what the Government has done has done to this country is wrong. The lack of respect that it has for the House of Commons, only a few years after being elected to government, is even worse. It is not right. We should not put up with it.
I say to the government Members across the way that it is their privileges as well as mine and, more important,

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
it is those privileges that have been vested in us by our constituents, the people who have sent us here.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my friend for Glengariy-Prescott-Russell. One reason the Government went the route of Governor General warrants was that it was afraid to face Parliament in February and March. Back in January, February and March merger mania going on in this country with Consolidated Bathurst, PWA, Labatt's Brewery and Carling O'Keefe. There were all kinds of mergers. The Government was on the wrong side of those issues, and the people of Canada were very concerned. They wanted us to ask questions in the House about those kinds of issues. Also, interest rates were going up, and the Government was talking about the deficit.
I wonder if the Member from the Liberal Party would agree with me that one reason why Parliament was not called back was that the Government was afraid to face Parliament, afraid to face the people of Canada. Parliament was supposed to come back on March 6. It delayed the recall of Parliament until April 3. Then on April Fool's Day we got a Governor General warrant asking for $6 billion. I think one reason we had a delay in the recall of Parliament was that it was afraid to come back and face the representatives of the people of Canada. This is why we had this very unconventional, very unconstitutional approach of seeking a Governor General warrant. This is riding roughshod over the traditions of Parliament. If John Diefenbaker were in the House today, he would be lecturing the Conservatives of the day.
Does my friend in the Liberal Party agree that the reason was not only a disrespect of Parliament, not only breaking the conventions and the rules of this place as we have practised them for many years, but that the Government was afraid to recall Parliament because the issues of the day were unpopular ones from the point of view of the Conservative Party?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious that the Government had reason to do it. There was something going through the back of its head, obviously.
When Parliament adjourned on December 30, that first part of not seeking supply at that time, there is no doubt that that is negligence. Someone probably goofed for that period of time. Of course we should be concerned about that goof-up. The Government went so far as to fail to ask for supply in the Throne Speech; it was that bad. Even worse, for that first period until December 30 it did not ask for any money. That was bad enough, but then it adjourned without having done so. That is worse. It was looking at the schedule in February, and the chairman of the Conservative caucus came out of caucus one day and announced brilliantly that the Government needed more recess time to prepare a Throne Speech. Of course, it had been elected since November 21 of the year before, but it needed more time to write, of all things, a Throne Speech. Perhaps the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wrote it on the back of an envelope on the way back from his constituency. Looking at what was in the Throne Speech, that is probably the process he utilized to prepare it.
Notwithstanding, in the month of February we had a Government overtaken by a very difficult situation. The Free Trade Deal had just recently passed. We saw mergers and closures of plants in Canada. We saw takeovers of Canadian industry. It was basically a very unpopular situation for the Government.
The Government looked at it and said: "Well, if we recall Parliament, we are really going to be in for it. The Opposition is going to be all over us. The Canadian media is going to be all over us. Why don't we just cool it for a while? Maybe the problem will go away."
That has been said by Tory Members before-"if you do not like the problem, just wait it out and it will disappear". They tried. However, they had a further problem, that is, if Parliament returned on March 6, not only would they have the regular eveiy day barrage of questions rightfully asking the Government to account, but they would have an even worse situation in their view where there would be only a short period of time left until the supply period ended. I think there was something like 12 sitting days of the House of Commons left in that supply period between March 6 and March 28.
Out of those 12 days the rules of this House say that we must have 9 days of supply. Those supply days constitute opposition debate in the House of Commons, or what we affectionately refer to as opposition days. Could we imagine how everything would have crashed on the head of the Government across the way? Notwithstanding, the Government had to get money. It had
May 15, 1989

to recall Parliament because it did not have any funds to operate.
Members across the way said to themselves: "Look, when we forgot during the Christmas period to ask the House of Commons for supply, we used the Governor General special warrant. That worked then. Why don't we use some more of them and forget about Parliament meeting altogether?" That is what they did. They waited until the new fiscal year of the Government in order to avoid the supply period and to avoid the debates that would have been coming their way in the House of Commons. That is really what happened.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am a little surprised by the action or the lack of action on the part of the Government because, as my hon. friend from Kingston and the Islands said this morning, this amendment is really not to condemn the Government. We are not pasting the Government to the wall over this. We are simply saying that this procedure may be wrong, that there is some doubt about it and we can remove that doubt by what we are doing in the House this afternoon.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nys-trom) talks about the late John Diefenbaker. I am sure that the late John Diefenbaker, if he were alive today, would be literally spinning hearing Members opposite. If there ever was a Canadian who believed in the supremacy of Parliament it certainly was the late Right Hon. John Diefenbaker.
I have a question for the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). Does he think we are condemning the Government or just simply asking the Government to remove this doubt that hangs over the procedure that it took? We are saying the Government may have made a mistake, that this is perhaps a wrong procedure. If the Government were not just so intransigent and stubborn it could agree and clear up the confusion.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all that I want from the Government across the way right now-and I have already aired the grievance in terms of supply, in terms of how wrong the Government was and so on-is to recognize that what the Government has utilized should
Appropriation Act
not constitute a precedent for the future. That is all I want from the Government across the way.
There are two ways of achieving it. One is through the amendment proposed to us by the other place. That is certainly the best way. But even if the Government does not do that, at least it should recognize in a motion or an amendment to the motion that what it has used should not constitute a precedent. I will not even say that what the Government has done is illegal, even though I think it is. I do not even want the motion from the Government to say that what it has done may have been unconstitutional. We will debate that later.
The Government needs that Bill and I recognize that. All I am asking from the Government pure and simply is for the Government to state that what it has done shall not constitute a precedent. If the Government is willing to do that, we could let this Bill go through and the Government could have the supply that it needs in order to administer the affairs of the nation. That is all the action that I am looking for, that recognition of non-precedence if you wish.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, actually it is kind of a sad day to be participating in this kind of a debate.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Why then speak?

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
My hon. friend says, "Why then speak?" I think that is the point. The Government would prefer not to have this procedure exposed. The Government would rather not have the people of Canada understand what it has done. I do not know if the Government has done this in a sneaky, sinister, mean-spirited, cruel way or if it is just incompetence or combinations thereof, Mr. Speaker. I do think that people watching and listening in to the proceedings of the House today will be aware of one thing, that something has occurred recently that has never occurred in our history before. Something has occurred in the last few weeks that has never occurred in any real parliamentary democracy anywhere in the world where the Government has decided that it knows best, that the Parliament of Canada does not know best, that the Parliament of Canada is a nuisance, that having an Opposition to deal with is a nuisance and so it was going to try to sneak something through. The Government was trying to do something very dishonourable, perhaps

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
illegal, certainly unconstitutional and unethical and unacceptable.
What has the Government actually done? The Government has decided to spend a lot of money. As a matter of fact, it comes to $295 for every single Canadian. The Government decided that it would spend $295 for every man, woman and child in this country, in secret, without ever telling Parliament what it is doing. I suspect that is why Canadians have a growing cynicism towards the Government. I think that the sense of disillusionment, disappointment, and the aggravation level is increasing so that it is now almost moving off the top of the barometer.
Here is a government that decided to break parliamentary tradition. This is a government that decided to abandon parliamentary procedure, to toss the traditions and experiences of parliamentary democracy out of the window for its own sneaky political purposes. This, of course, as you well know, being a concerned parliamentarian yourself, is nothing new. This Government has developed a reputation for abusing Parliament, of taking advantage of various interpretations of various rules or, simply by strength of numbers, changing the rules to its own satisfaction. This Government has a certain political agenda and when it runs up against a House of Commons which might prohibit it from doing something, the Government says, "Let us not worry about tradition, practice, rules and regulations, but use our majority to unilaterally change the rules to suit our own agenda".
Not long ago the Government decided that the Standing Orders which govern the House of Commons would not enable it to do something very abusive, so it said it would not worry but simply change the rules. We know that over the last hundred and some years when the rules of the House of Commons have been changed it was done in consultation with all of the players. In other words, as parliamentarians, this is our House. It is not simply a tool of the Government. We would sit and sometimes take many weeks and months to agree to change the rules to suit doing the business of the country. But that was not done this time. It would take too long, so the Government said it would change the rules any way it liked and if the Opposition did not like it, tough luck.
We remember the Free Trade Agreement. This is when we came back after the election and the Government did something unprecedented in Canadian history. It used, if you like, the muzzle of closure at every single stage of the Free Trade Agreement. This has never been done before in Canadian history because most Governments welcome debate. They realize that part of the parliamentary system is to have debate at various crucial stages of a BUI. But not this Government. It said no. This Government decided to use closure at every single opportunity so that it could muzzle Parliament, neuter Parliament, and not allow Parliament to carry out its duties and responsibilities expected by the people. Actually, I have a long list of instances where the Government abused Parliament, but I think I have made my point.
This is part of a trend, a new way of doing business. It is a parliamentary bully technique that if you do not like what is going on you just bully your way through and ignore the traditions of the House.
There are a number of things Members have indicated they have found very offensive about this situation. When Parliament was recalled to deal with the Free Trade Agreement in December, did the Government ask for the passage of a Supply Bill to allow it to receive parliamentary permission to carry out its various activities? No, it did not do that. The Government just simply prorogued Parliament and people left for Christmas. Then, in January the Government decided it needed some money. The parliamentary, traditional and proper thing to do, which has always been done over the years, would be to recall Parliament to pass a Supply Bill. That is the way it is done so that the people of Canada through their elected representatives have a voice in the affairs of the country. That was not done. A Governor General Special Warrant was introduced by the Government for $80 million in secret, behind closed doors, so that Canadians would not be aware of what it was doing. Then on February 16 another Special Warrant was issued for $500 million. Rather than do the right thing, that is, introduce legislation in this House, the Government is using this back door, under the table, kind of sneaky, dishonest approach.
Now why were they doing that? I remember those of us on the opposition benches were asking the Speaker to reconvene the House. There were major issues facing the country. The fall-out from the free trade deal was already beginning to be felt, as hundreds of jobs were starting to disappear as a result of firms enacting the free trade provisions. We saw a whole rash of very unproductive mergers, takeovers and acquisitions take place. We called for a special debate to understand what was going on, whether our existing legislation would serve the country during this time of mega-merger activity. But, no, Mr. Speaker, again there was no interest in recalling
May 15, 1989

Parliament. Remember that interest rates were starting to increase significantly.
Then there was the whole matter of American Express instantly becoming a bank because the Minister of Finance thought this was a way to pay off the American Express people who supported the free trade deal with the United States.
I could go on. There were all sorts of very important, critical issues facing the countiy, and we asked for Parliament to be reconvened to debate these matters and to provide an opportunity for the Government to bring in its supply motion because we recognized there was a need to expend funds. That was not done. Rather than do the honourable thing, the Government on March 23 again issued another special warrant for $891 million.
Before I get to the big special warrant of $6 billion, something very sinister happened. I want to appeal to my good associate and friend, the government House Leader. The House Leaders met on a number of occasions to agree in principle to a schedule for the debate on the passage of supply. A date was agreed upon. A special order was agreed upon so that the Government would know that its special passage of supply would occur at a certain time. After that fact, the Government still went ahead with the special warrants: $891 million, and then finally on April 1, $6 billion-$6 billion of expenditures without ever hearing a single voice from Canada's Parliament.
Where does this end? We say to the Government that we recognize now that this is how it is going to do business. There is no need to recall Parliament for most of the year. In terms of its supply legislation, it could just handle the whole matter through Governor General warrants.
This is a very serious situation. The whole matter of the last two special warrants occurred after the House was actually scheduled to resume. We agreed that March
Appropriation Act
6 would be the appropriate time, but even after that date, the special Governor General warrants occurred.
There is no way to describe it other than trampling on the rights of Parliament. That is very clear to all of us. One of the aspects of our parliamentary system that we feel very strongly about is that Parliament must remain supreme. For hundreds of years that tradition has grown. We are not a republic. We are not run on laws; we are run on tradition. We are run on practice. Over the years certain ways of conducting the business of the people of Canada have evolved. We follow those traditions. So we know from year to year, from decade to decade what to expect in terms of the process and procedure. The principle of Parliament being supreme has been with us for hundreds of years. The raising of revenues, the expenditures associated with those revenues must exist with Parliament and not with the Cabinet, not with the executive and not through the use of special Governor General warrants.
In conclusion, I believe that the Government has abused the Financial Administration Act that, in a sense, gave them the authority to proceed this way. There are times, we agree, when there is a necessity to use a Governor General warrant. Let us be very clear about that. We are not suggesting that there never has existed a time for this type of initiative. Usually it is associated with an election campaign, where it is impossible to recall the House of Commons to deal with this kind of a financial issue.
Beyond that, Mr. Speaker, when we were willing, able and interested in sitting in Parliament in January, February and March, why did the Government then not do the traditional and honour bound thing is what we are raising today.
I have some concerns, as do my colleagues, that the Senate is not the institution to influence legislation in a serious way. However, in this case, they sent it back for some reconsideration. At the time I remember making a case with other Hon. Members that this process that the Government used was unacceptable and inappropriate, that Parliament had been duped and that there had been an end run occurring around the parliamentary system.
As Hon. Members in this House, we had made an agreement. We had passed a special order. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that we appealed to the Chair to see

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
if circumstances had changed from when we had first agreed to that special order. We had questioned whether this was an appropriate step to take under the circumstances of these Governor General warrants being issued. The Speaker, with all due respect, found that it was appropriate and we proceeded. Now we have an opportunity to send a very clear signal to this Government that what it has done is not acceptable. What it has done has set a very dangerous precedent. What it has done is unconventional and ought to be unacceptable to any serious-minded parliamentarian.
We will be here for a few moments longer, and I hope that members from the government benches will stand and explain how, now that we have broken the tradition of hundreds of years of parliamentary democracy, why they would support this motion. We have given them a way out that I think is acceptable by proposing an amendment to the Government's motion which I think makes it acceptable to all Members. While what has occurred may respect the letter of the law, that is not what we are debating here. Legally I suspect that one could make a case that the Government has not broken the law, but they have broken every tradition that this House stands for. For that reason, we say in our amendment that the action of the Government may respect the letter of the law, but the action is unconventional, and it sets a very dangerous precedent. Any serious-minded parliamentarian would have to agree with that, and we look forward perhaps to a unanimous vote on the amendment later in the day.

He did not use the word criminal, but he used the words "sinister and devious act to deprive the people of Canada of billions of dollars of public resources that did not receive the scrutiny of the people's representatives". The people of this country need to know that all that the Government has done is pay its bills and live up to the obligations that this House has created for the people of Canada, at the encouragement of some of the people in the Opposition. I do not recall a single Bill in the last two years where we brought forward some measure where the Opposition has not said, you are not spending enough. They want another $4 billion for day care.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It is not your money.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
They cannot have it both ways. We pay our bills, as painful as it is, with the $320 billion debt. But they come back and say, you spent too much. You pay the bills as if they are our bills. There is not a single penny that has been spent with the Governor General warrants that has had anything to do with discretionary spending.
When the unemployment insurance cheques or pension cheques bounce, the people of Canada will judge how sinister this move was. This is utterly ridiculous.
I ask the Hon. Member to be fair and honest. What we have done is legal and provided for in the statutes. The warrants allow us the resources to do what this Parliament and the country has been obligating us to do. That is all we were trying to do. I ask The Hon. Member to see his way clear to being as fair as he tended to be at the end of his remarks when he said that everything that was done was within the law. He also said that this was not a precedent. It has been done many times before. That is why there is provision for the Governor General warrant. Why can the Hon. Member not be honest, and at least not use words such as "sinister" and "devious". Nothing in this measure is devious. Not a single penny has been spent on any discretionary programs. All of it is required to be spent under the Order that was previously passed, debated, and voted on in the House. All we are doing is paying the bills with which the Opposition helped us to encumber the Canadian people.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I appreciate the intervention of my hon. friend. He states that I have used the terms: "sinister, unconventional, sneaky, under the table, end run, and devious". The only reason I used those words is that I could not think of other related terms.
For example, what were some of those funds used for? Most Canadians have been offended of late by that old coin rolling out on television screens to remind us that the Government is blaming Canadians for being irresponsible for many years. We know who is making the
May 15, 1989

decisions on how the money is to be spent, and that is the Government.
For example, the Minister of the Environment thought that he should spend some money redecorating his office. My hon. friend tells me that it was $40,000. The Prime Minister thought that some evaluation needed to be done to the landscaping at 24 Sussex Drive, and some major renovations. Of course, there was also $2.7 million worth of advertising. Presumably these are the items that the Minister says were important.
I also wish to remind the Minister that in most countries, governments have to vote supply before the House is adjourned. They do it in the correct order.
I also wish to remind the Minister that, after the new fiscal year began, before we had the Estimates in our hands to find out how the Government was going to spend the taxpayers' money, the Government decided to use a special warrant of $6 billion. In other words, it had decided that before the House of Commons even looked at an Estimate it had decided how it was going to be spent. This is very serious when one considers what the Government is using it for.
Eugene Forsey is unquestionably recognized as an expert in the field of parliamentary procedure and constitutional law. He indicated very clearly that this was unconventional, unusual, and unacceptable. He also stated that he could probably make a very strong case that it was unconstitutional and that the Constitution of the country had been ignored in this process. Let us forget that, and say that perhaps there is some legal case that can be made that what the Government has actually done is to use the Financial Administration Act in a way it was never intended.
I wish to remind my hon. friend, the Minister, that when warrants have been used in the past it has been because Parliament was not sitting or was unable to sit. For example, one understands that during or immediately after an election, the Government is not in a position to have a financial plan before it. However, this was months after an election. This was after Parliament had already sat in December. Parliament could have sat in January, February, or March.
However, rather than convene Parliament to deliberate on the appropriate ways to collect taxes and expend revenues, which is after all why we are here, the Government decided that it knew best. It was not going to use the parliamentary process, or the time honoured
Appropriation Act
tradition developed over hundreds of years, and that it had a better way.
That is why I called it sinister, indecent, unconventional, unacceptable, and inappropriate. I could continue with a long list of other terms to describe how parliamentarians who have thought about this process feel about it, and how most Canadians, once they become aware of what the Government has done, would also describe this action of the Government on this particular issue.

It would fall upon all of us to examine it in that light. In a calm and deliberate way, hopefully I can restore some balance to this discussion. What the Hon. Member for Kamloops and other Members in the Opposition do not seem to understand is that it was not the House of Commons' action that was unprecedented. It was the process leading up to that situation that was unprecedented.
As Members will recall, there was an election on November 21,1988. We met as soon as possible after that election to deal with the major subject matter of the election which was the Free Trade Agreement. We gathered in the House and dealt with free trade expeditiously, winding up on Christmas Eve. I did not hear any Member of the House rise and state: "I do not want to go home for Christmas. I do not want to spend some time in my constituency". We dealt with the business at hand and all Members departed. I have here a copy of the House of Commons Debates from that time. No member of the Opposition stood up on Christmas Eve and suggested that we continue the House to deal with financial matters or Estimates. Nothing was said.
On December 16 in that very session the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) tabled Supplementary Estimates B and things carried on in the normal way. When the House was not sitting, during what would be a normal recess period, a Governor General warrant was obtained in accordance with the law passed by the Parliament of Canada and the Financial Administration Act. It was reported in The Canada Gazette. The warrant was granted on January 16,1989, reported in The Canada Gazette 12 days later. Did anyone hear the Hon. Member

May 15, 1989
Appropriation Act
for Kamloops stand up and say: "What is this warrant reported in The Canada Gazette? I want to examine this". Did Members of the Liberal Party complain at that point? Did they demand any more information? It was public knowledge. No, they were quite satisfied that the law had been followed. If they were not, they certainly did not complain about it.

I hope you will take into account, Mr. Speaker, that that interruption cut into my train of thought. I will have to re-explain this whole situation so Members opposite will understand clearly, because they do not get the point.
The law has been followed. There is no other law. There could be some other law. On another day or at another time there may evolve and develop a constitutional question. However, that is for the Supreme Court of Canada to determine. Every Member of the Liberal Party must remember 1981 when they said there was no constitutional convention and the Supreme Court of
Canada said there was. How did that determination get made? Because the case was taken to the Supreme Court of Canada. If Members opposite do not like the law, I suggest that they take the case to the Supreme Court of Canada.
I hope the Hon. Member from Kamloops realizes what havoc he may wreak across Canada if he and his colleagues persist in this legal game that they are playing. What will happen to pension cheques, veterans cheques, and the payments required from the Government of Canada and the interest that builds up?
If the Hon. Member objects at this time and place in the House of Commons to the process that has been followed, where was he in January when those warrants were published in The Canada Gazette and made public knowledge to all Canadians?
Why did he not raise the objection then? Why did he not demand that Parliament be recalled to deal with the matter then? Where was he then? He talks a lot now but it may be too late.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say in response to my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby), that most of us would have enjoyed the opportunity to raise the matter in Parliament when we read it in The Gazette in January, but the point is that we were not sitting.

I was coming to that, Mr. Speaker. I will deal with it in a minute.
We had hoped that this matter could be dealt with quickly so that it could go back to the Senate and those people who rely on discretionary cheques from the Government of Canada would be able to get their cheques tomorrow. As a result of the actions of the Opposition and the other place, which I will get to in a minute, that is not possible.
I rise to refute all the allegations of illegality and to put on the record for the people of Canada just how long my friends opposite have been thrashing around with a non-issue. First, there was a point of order considered by the Chair on April 6. We spent over an hour debating it, which we do not object to at all.
Appropriation Act
On Tuesday, May 2, the Speaker ruled that there was no case for illegality to be made in this place and that if my hon. friends wanted to take this up they should take it up somewhere else.
On Thursday, May 4, in the middle of a vote while Members from all Parties were trying to meet then-planes, because these votes proceed very quickly under normal circumstances, there was another point of order. It was also ruled out of order by the Chair.
We take the position that the use of special warrants during adjournments is allowed by law. Lest anybody suggest that there is a convention that this is not done, let me point out to the House that in 1951, when the Financial Administration Act was passed, there was an amendment specifically to allow for the use of special warrants during adjournments.
I think the comments of the Deputy Minister of Finance at that time are illustrative of why it is now legal and why the change was made in the Financial Administration Act. The Deputy Minister of Finance stated:
This provision is made necessary by the practice which has developed in recent years of long adjournments.
The next day during clause-by-clause consideration there was little discussion on this clause. There was no concern raised on this clause in the House of Commons. It is apparent from this discussion that Parliament was well aware of the new provision, and it meant that special warrants would be used at times other than immediately prior to or after an election.
Officials from the Department of Justice have considered this matter. They have found that the warrants in this case have been used properly. Much was made by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Mr. Milliken) of the comments by Dr. Forsey during his testimony at the Senate's Finance Committee. I cautioned him fairly when he was speaking. I raised this piece of paper, hoping he would get to the remarks written here and properly illustrate all of the remarks of Dr. Forsey. Unfortunately he did not do so.
I want to read into the record exactly what Dr. Forsey said:
Assuming this is perfectly legal, and I suspect it is, the legality of it would not be questioned. It is absolutely essential to draw the distinction between legality and constitutional propriety. I said it was legal under the statute, subject to the caution that Senator Frith

May 15, 1989

Appropriation Act
made and that I said, in my amateur, lay way, that I agreed with, I think it was legal.
He went on:
That is the point that Senator Frith made, and I said that I was inclined to agree that there was some legal doubt about it. However, it seems to me that the essential question is not the strictly legal question at all.
Unfortunately, my hon. friend did not allude to those points.

The Law Clerk of the Senate, in referring to this amendment that was sent to us by the Senate, said:
As Counsel to the Senate, I have a problem with the amendment. I find it improper to imply in an amendment that actions authorized by Parliament under a provision of law would be illegal. So I have a problem with the wording. The committee has gone over the three tests in section 30 of the Financial Administration Act that were discussed yesterday. No one has any problem with the first test -
Mr. du Plessis went on to say that: "The law, according to its own terms, has been complied with".
Lest anyone suggest that the Government was judging itself when the Ministry of Justice officials looked at this, we took the precaution of going to an outside expert. We have a written opinion by a recognized constitutional expert, professor Peter Hogg of Osgoode Hall Law School, to the effect that special warrants as issued were legal.
This has all been very interesting. In closing, let me just ask what are the legal force and effect of the delaying tactics of the Opposition? What are the legal force and effect of the delaying tactics of the Senate?
The Senate had a tough day. It sat from 2 p.m. to 2.15 p.m. These are the people who the Official Opposition are rushing to support. These are the people who the NDP, which refuses to have anything to do with the Senate, rush to support. They had a tough 15-minute workday.
The rest of us and the people out there who rely on these payments that will not be made tomorrow because of their actions work a little longer than 15 minutes a day. The effect is that the non-elected, appointed Liberal Senate has delayed this Bill by putting through this amendment. They were joined in this action by the Opposition.
Had they sat a little longer today and had this not been filibustered by my friends opposite, the Senate might have had the Bill today.
As well, those discretionary payments that will stop at midnight tonight could be made.
I suggest that this has all been a farce created by the other place, joined in gleefully by my friends opposite, without any thought about the practical effect on the people whom they were elected to serve. I cannot say that about the Senate since Senators are not appointed to serve anybody except the Liberal Party. I am surprised that the NDP has been rushing to join the Liberal Party in this venture. However, they are now joined in a common cause-support of the Liberal Senate.
I suggest that Members opposite call back to their ridings tonight to explain this to the folks who should be getting those discretionary cheques. If they push it any longer through Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday, they should explain this to the veterans and members of the RCMP. It was voted on by Parliament to supply that funding. Every legal expert we can find says it is legal. My friends opposite say that it was illegal. They want to filibuster this even longer. I suggest that there will be a difficult task back home.
It is a lot of fun here for them. We have debated it. My colleagues will get together on Wednesday in the Liberal caucus room. Unfortunately, my hon. friend from Kamloops will be excluded because he won't be in the Liberal caucus room. Lord knows he should be after today. They will sit there and the MacEachens and the Friths of this world will say: "Boy, did we pull one over on the people this week. They will not get paid". Just come right out, folks, and tell them why they will not get paid. It is because appointed Senators down the way who had a 15-minute workday were responsible for them not getting paid. They were joined by the Liberal Opposition in the House of Commons and the NDP.
I submit everything we have done is legal. Surely, that is what it is all about. I suggest we get on with the business of the nation.

If there are any problems in terms of paycheques getting out to the right people at the right time, it is because the Government has bungled the business of Canada. The President of the Treasury Board says that he followed the law. The point is that if Members of the Government had done what has always been done, we would not be here today. This debate would not have occurred today if that were done. The House of Commons would have voted on the appropriate terms of supply, and the business would have been done as it has
been done in parliamentary democracies for hundreds of years.
However, members of the Government decided to take a short-cut. They decided to do an end run around Parliament, to do something under the table, to sneak something through.
All we are saying is that if the Government had the courage, the decency and the honour to do things appropriately and the way Canadians want them to be done, this would not have occurred. The Minister of Justice should be honest and say: "Yes, we have made a mistake. We have made an error in judgment. We did something rather dastardly when it comes to parliamentary process. We should not have done it". He will have an opportunity shortly to vote on a very reasoned amendment which would allow the Government to say that the letter of the law may in fact have been kept but that what it has done as a Government is unconventional and sets a very dangerous precedent.
I know that the Minister of Justice and the President of the Treasury Board, being the kind of people that they are, will agree that what has been done is unconventional and that what the Government has done is in fact setting a very dangerous precedent. I look forward to their support when we vote on the amendment.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will return to the borrowing Bill, another integral part of the Budget process. This Budget is a milestone for the future of Canada. It marks the point where Canada as a nation recognized that there is a threat to our way of life. It also marks the point where we started to effectively deal with it. It marks the point where we took action as a
Borrowing Authority
Government and as a people to maintain our standard of living and our social programs, not just for ourselves but for our children as well.
The Progressive Conservative Government has been working since 1984 to get the threat of debt under control. This took tough action, competent management of the economy, and strong control of government spending. We succeeded in cutting the deficit by $9.5 billion and by slowing the rate of growth of the debt from 24 per cent a year to less than 10 per cent last year. Despite this progress the public debt is still growing faster than our ability to carry it. That is why the Budget proposes some strong medicine to face up to the debt challenge.
The reality is that we still have a long way to go. Today we are debating the approval of a Bill to permit the Government to borrow $25.55 billion. This will permit the Government to meet its financial requirements and to conduct foreign exchange operations.
Perhaps some background would be helpful. In general, the Government requires parliamentary authority to borrow new money. A notable exception is temporary loans under Section 47 of the Financial Administration Act with a maturity of less than six months when there are insufficient funds to meet disbursements. With the exception of these special Section 47 loans new parliamentary authority is not required to roll over existing debt.
The deficit is projected to be $30.5 billion in the 1989-90 fiscal year, compared to $38.3 billion in the 1984-85 fiscal year. However, this is not equal to the borrowing requirements of the Government for three reasons.
First, the Government has access to $10.4 billion in non-budgetary sources of funding such as contributions to the Public Service superannuation accounts. The projected financial requirements after taking non-budgetary items into account are $20.5 billion.
Second, foreign exchange operations will affect the Government's borrowing requirements. For example, when the Canadian Government acts to moderate a rise in the Canadian dollar, Canadian dollars must be borrowed while the acquired U.S. dollars are added to our foreign exchange reserves.

May 15, 1989
Burrowing Authority
A $3 billion borrowing authority reserve will be sought to provide for flexibility in managing foreign exchange transactions including exchange fund earnings.
Third, the amount that must be borrowed is increased by the exchange fund earnings.
The exchange fund earnings are related to the investment income from Canada's foreign exchange holdings, particularly in the form of U.S. dollar denominated assets. Since these earnings are in foreign currency, they increased the reported level of foreign exchange holdings but do not reduce financial requirements even though they are reported as budget revenues. Exchange fund earnings are projected to be $1.3 billion.
On March 31 of the previous fiscal year, the Government used its emergency borrowing powers under Section 47 of the Financial Administration Act to borrow $750 million. This Bill will refinance this temporary debt and authorize a further $24.8 billion for a total of $25.55 billion, consisting of, as I have noted, the 1989-90 financial requirements of $20.5 billion, exchange fund earnings of $1.3 billion, a reserve of $3 billion and the replenishment of Section 47 loans for another $750 million for a total of $25.55 billion.
The Government's financial requirements are a comprehensive measure of the demands on credit markets. These requirements have fallen sharply from $29.8 billion in 1984-85 to a projected $20.5 billion in 1989-90. Relative to the size of the economy, financial requirements have fallen from 6.7 per cent of gross domestic product to a projected 3.2 per cent this year. By 1993-94 the Government's financial requirements will have fallen to $3 billion or 0.3 per cent of gross domestic product.
To accomplish this we have made and will continue to make some tough choices. That is what we were elected to do. We have striven to ensure that the total budget package has an appropriate balance that reflects regional circumstances and a greater burden on those who are able to cany it.
On the expenditure side of the ledger, the work of the Expenditure Review Committee of Cabinet has resulted in major reductions of Government spending which add up to about $2.5 billion per year. This builds on the efforts we have made in the past four years to reduce program spending as a portion of the economy from 19.5
per cent when we took office to 16 per cent this year and about 15 per cent by 1993-94.
Since 1984, this Government has worked to build a strong foundation on which Canadians could achieve their economic potential. Over the past four years, the Government has introduced a number of structural policies and reforms that raise the prospects for growth and higher living standards for Canadians. We modernized the regulatory environment for business. We reformed the corporate and personal income tax systems to make them more equitable and to increase the incentives to save and invest. We negotiated the Cana-da-U.S. Trade Agreement, which by securing access to the large U.S. market will permit Canadian firms to operate on a larger, more efficient scale and seek expanded markets for their products.
We encouraged research and development and approved job training programs. We replaced the Foreign Investment Review Agency with Investment Canada to encourage the foreign investment that provides net benefits to Canada.
Together with responsible fiscal actions, our economic measures created a climate in which Canadians could face the economic challenges of a tough competitive world.
We will also continue our privatization efforts, including the sale of the remaining Air Canada shares, the sale of two former divisions of Atomic Energy of Canada and a stepped up evaluation of other possible privatization candidates.
Our earlier efforts to make the Post Office self-sufficient have succeeded. Not only did it make a profit last year, the Post Office will start paying dividends to the Government.
These efforts to make sure tax dollars are spent wisely would not be complete unless transfers to individuals were also examined. For example, as the Hon. Member for Edmonton Northwest (Mr. Dorin) has pointed out, senior citizen's pensions represent the largest single expenditure of Government, in the neighbourhood of $15 billion a year. Those pensions are indexed so that every year the amount we spend on them will increase by the amount of inflation, which is currently running about 4 per cent. So we have an approximate 4 per cent increase simply as a result of that. Second, the population is growing older. There are more and more people turning 65 and entitled to these pensions. The result of inflation and more people turning 65 will require the Government to find an additional $1.5 billion this year
May 15, 1989

just to maintain the existing program-not to improve it, enhance it or increase it. Our seniors will not be denied their due. Our seniors will not be penalized because they did not have the opportunities of this generation.
Canada's social safety net is important to all of us and it must be preserved and made secure for now and the future. That means that the priority purposes of programs like old age security and family allowance must be to assist lower and middle-income Canadians, not to unnecessarily subsidize those with higher incomes. That is why the Budget proposes to use the tax system to recover these payments from high income taxpayers. Those with individual net incomes greater than $50,000 will repay these benefits or part of them. Everyone eligible will continue to receive a cheque. This repayment measure will ensure that those who need assistance will retain their benefits, and those with high incomes will repay more as their income rises.
The Budget also contains tax increases. Higher revenues will contribute to narrowing the imbalance between government income and outgo so that this generation pays for today's programs and contributes to debt control. This will return total revenues as a share of the economy to levels that prevailed in the early 1970s before deficits started to balloon out of control when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) was Finance Minister.
Let us remember that when the Leader of the Opposition was Finance Minister the deficit increased by $4 billion. Relative to the size of the economy the deficit doubled from 1.6 per cent of Gross Domestic Product to 3.3 per cent. In contrast, the present Minister of Finance has cut the deficit by $10 billion and relative to the GDP the deficit has been almost cut in half from 8.6 per cent to 4.9 per cent. When the Leader of the Opposition was Finance Minister total spending rose by 107 per cent in four years. That is four times faster than the spending increases of the present Government. If the Minister of Finance had increased his spending at the same rate as the then Minister of Finance, taxes this year would have had to double just to keep the deficit from rising.
Borrowing Authority
Some would argue that the Government has taken harsh measures to tackle the deficit. But this Government has also helped ease the tax load on many Canadians. The refundable federal sales tax credit for adults and children will be doubled to protect those with low incomes. The income threshold will also be increased to $18,000. This means a single person with an income of $18,000 will receive $140 credit next year, and a family of four will receive $420. This measure provides substantial assistance to those most in need.
A further part of our debt control strategy relates to the unemployment insurance system. The changes announced recently to improve the UI program, increased training and improved the equity and incentive provisions, were designed to redirect resources within the program.
At the same time changes will be made to ensure that the financing of the program is consistent with our efforts to control the debt. Beginning in 1990 the UIC system will be fully financed by employer and employee premiums. The Government will continue to finance the UIC account should it go into deficit and difficult times.
A major part of this strategy is the reform of the federal sales tax. A new tax called the goods and services tax will replace the current system on January 1, 1991. It will have a broad base and will have a rate of 9 per cent.
Sales tax reform has been in the works for a long time. The present tax is hidden, unfair and damaging to our economy. While the joint federal-provincial reform of the Senate is not possible at this time, the importance of the reform made it necessary for the federal Government to move ahead. The new goods and services tax will provide a more stable revenue base for government programs and debt control.
It will improve the over-all fairness of the tax system. It will be more visible to the consumer than the current federal sales tax and it will allow the economy to function more efficiently. The goods and services tax will be levied on a vast majority of goods and services consumed in Canada. However, basic groceries, prescription drugs and medical devices will not be taxed. Residential rents, child care, legal aid and most health, educational and dental services will also be tax exempt. The paper burden on small business will be minimized.

May 15, 1989
Burrowing Authority
The 9 per cent rate will provide sufficient revenues to replace the existing federal sales tax, allow income tax reductions for middle-income households and provide a new refundable sales tax credit. This credit will be paid four times a year in advance of the start of the new tax and will be designed to ensure that families earning less than $30,000 will be better off as a result of sales tax reform.
The combination of spending costs and tax increases today in the reform of the sales tax system in 1991 will make sure that the threat of the debt is dealt with decisively. The challenge is to make sure that we keep to this task each year, every year until the job is done.
This Budget puts us on the right course, with an improved ability as a nation to carry the debt, with a strengthened capacity to maintain vital social and cultural programs and other important public services. With prudent fiscal management and reduced spending, I hope by the fourth year of this mandate that we will not need to borrow to pay our bills. I wish we did not have to borrow, but that is the legacy of our debt. That is why this Budget is about building for the future, not borrowing from it. That is why the Budget deals firmly with the major obstacle to a better future, the problem of our growing debt. This Budget is designed to overcome that obstacle. The measures in it are tough. They have to be to match the challenges we are facing.

Mr. Speaker, I listened intently to my hon. friend from Calgary, and I found his remarks interesting. There is an apparent contradiction which I would like to point out. He talks about himself and his Party defending Canada's social programs, and states that they are as concerned about our social programs as we are on this side of the House. I wonder how he can say that, given the fact that they have introduced this Draconian measure in the Budget called the claw-back, which in effect puts an end to universality in this country.
If I said to my hon. friends across the way that if we were introducing a Canada-wide pension plan or Canada-wide family allowance, and providing those programs only to those people earning $10,000 or $15,000 a year, they would say, "Oh, no, that is a form of welfare, and
we would not stand for that". But that is exactly what this Government is proposing to do. They are starting at the other end, and coming down.
It has already been pointed out a number of times in this House that if this Government can start at $70,000 in clawing back pensions, clawing back the family allowance, it can do it at $60,000, $50,000, $40,000 or $20,000. That is the direction it is taking. Not only that, if it can do it with pensions, it can do it with medicare.
When it comes to Conservative thinking, if the Government wants to reduce the deficit by cutting back on pensions, would it not include cutting back on medicare benefits? It seems to me that that is what it can do.
The point I really want to make is this. One of the unique features of universality is bringing rich and poor together in the same constituency. By dividing those people through a claw-back measure, the rich people in this country begin to resent the payments to the people who are at the lower end of the pay scales. Pretty soon there will be no support from that constituency of Canadians for pensions and family allowances.
People who are fairly well off in this country do not lend the same support to welfare as they might do to pensions because they do not see anything in it for themselves. It is a welfare measure that has become stigmatized.
Does my hon. friend from Calgary understand that people who are better off in this country will begin to resent pensions and family allowances that they themselves will never share in? They will pay into it but they will not share in something that should belong to them as a right of citizenship.

Regional Development
ments. The motion that we are dealing with is very important. If one looks at the history of regional economic development in this country, one sees why the issue itself is important.
First, in our Constitution regional development is specifically listed as a requirement of the House of Commons and the Parliament of Canada.
Second, over years of Liberal and Conservative government there has been a move away from a Department which was specifically responsible for regional economic expansion to the present Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, and now the Conservative Government is moving further in that direction by setting up a new Department with no specific mandate in its title for regional development.

When the Liberal Government disbanded the Department of Regional Economic Expansion it made a mistake. That mistake is still hurting the regions today. That approach does not work. It is especially harmful to the underdeveloped regions of the countiy. It is extremely hard on Atlantic Canada. I would argue that it does not have the same powers as a full-fledged Department. It does not have the staff of a full-fledged Department. It does not have the opportunity, the capacity, or the willingness to deal with other Departments in the way that the former Department of
