It does not have the same role within the whole budgetary process as other Departments.
The same thing could be said for the western diversification fund. In itself it can be a useful tool, but it cannot replace a Department which is specifically responsible for economic expansion and economic development in our nation.
If Members from the various regions think about that, they will realize that it is true. Those of us who have worked in Ottawa for a number of years know how important it is to have someone who is here making decisions, and how important it is to have someone here who has a voice.
I have already indicated that the voice is no longer there within Cabinet. I have already indicated that we do not have a voice at the Deputy Minister level, at Assistant Deputy Minister level, or other levels which are parallel to the aligned Departments. As a result we really have a situation where, as my colleague from Prince Albert-Churchill River indicated a few moments ago, we do not know if we are dealing with a political slush fund or a sense of government direction.
Certainly people who receive money for their projects, industries, corporations, and communities are very happy when they receive that money. Those who do not receive money are obviously not nearly as happy.
The problem that we and Members from Atlantic Canada have is that they cannot look at a clear mandate of what the Government is attempting to achieve. We do not know what the mandate of ACOA will be one year from now. We do not know what will happen to the money that is not spent through ACOA. We know that some of the projects that are funded seem to come out of nowhere, and the money has gone to nowhere and no jobs have been created. We could go through a whole list of embarrassing situations.
May 15, 1989

A government Member may rise and indicate that there are some rosy pictures from one or two of the grants. I would hope that when he rises he will also deal with the other grants and programs that did not prove to be fruitful. In terms of balance, he should do that.
However, my primary concern in presenting this motion is to indicate how we as a Parliament have failed in allowing the Government to go in this direction. The prior Liberal Government and the present Conservative Government made a tragic mistake in terms of understanding what our regions need.
In a previous speech I indicated that there was a House of Commons committee that was specifically responsible for regional economic expansion. That committee was able to travel. I took great pleasure in travelling with that committee when I was a member. We went into northern New Brunswick, Newfoundland, and other parts of Canada. As a Member from western Canada, on those trips I learned a lot about why programs were necessary and I also learned a lot about the communities we were in. I learned about some of the problems the Department of Regional Economic Expansion were having and what changes were needed to specific legislation, programs, and regulations. That is where we are failing at this point. There is no such standing committee of the House.
Therefore many Members of Parliament are not in a position to know what should be done in terms of changing government programs. Since there is no Minister directly responsible for regional development who can report to any committee of the House of Commons, the House of Commons cannot look at the whole scope of regional development programs in the budgetary process.
While specific agencies have particular responsibilities for regional development and can report that to the House, it is not like looking at the whole picture from coast to coast. That is what we need.
Newly elected Members were not here when we had the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I can say there is a significant difference from what is happening in the Standing Committees now and what happened eight or nine years ago when that Department existed.
Regional Development
The ability of Parliament to influence government programs has diminished as a result. While Members can examine the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agencies and deal with its mandate, the mandate is no where near that of the previous Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
Furthermore, the committee does not have the mandate to direct the efforts of the Government toward such things as reducing economic disparities or affecting over-all government regional economic policy. I can use those same arguments with regard to the western diversification fund.
That is the purpose of this motion. I hope Members opposite will not simply rise to speak about the grand successes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agencies or the wonderful achievements of the western diversification fund but will talk about what Parliament wants for regional development. I hope they will say what we should be doing in the House of Commons to represent the needs of those in the regions of Canada who are in most need of government assistance.
I remind Members opposite that this is a Private Member's Motion and does not require solidarity with the Government. It is an opportunity for them to speak about their region and their responsibility as a Member of Parliament. I hope Members opposite take that approach when they rise to speak.
The Government's policies mean that there are a number of issues which can no longer be raised in specific Standing Committees. This has concerned me particularly since I became our caucus spokesperson for Atlantic Canada issues. The mandate of the former Standing Committee on Regional Economic Expansion allowed us to cover the whole gambit of economic development in a certain region. While a Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans dealt with matters specifically concerning the fishery, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion could deal with the question of the Atlantic fishery within the scope of Department of Regional Economic Expansion estimates. It was possible to deal with regional issues concerning forestry, post-secondary education, transportation or native people in Atlantic Canada under the mandate of the Standing Committee on Regional Economic Expansion.

May 15, 1989
Regional Development
These concerns came within the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
When we visited northern New Brunswick, Comer Brook and St. John's East, we were given a royal reception because the people there wanted that direct input with Members of Parliament. They knew the importance of talking to Members of Parliament. They knew the importance of having a Department that would look at transportation, fisheries, and economic development as a whole rather than in isolation. We knew that the witnesses who would appear before the committee, whether in Campbellton or Comer Brook, would be involved in all aspects of the economy including the social programs of the regions.
This over-all perspective made a lot more sense not only to the MPs who were on the committee or to those who were listening to the presentations, but it made much more sense in helping the Government formulate its goals for that region. It made a lot of sense to have a Department of Regional Economic Expansion which could deal with numerous issues, including the fishery, post-secondary education, whether community colleges provided adequate courses for the people in that region, or whether there was the community infrastructure to attract industries.
That has gone out the window. It is a sad commentary on what has happened. We know that this was the agenda of senior bureaucrats in Ottawa in the early 1980s. They said so during hearings with the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and in a separate committee hearing dealing with industry and trade. They did not like having to encourage corporations to set up in particular areas such as Campbellton, Summerside, Halifax or Cape Breton because it should not be their responsibility to direct private enterprise. They would rather have the programs in place and leave it to the companies to decide where they wanted to set up.
That was a hard concept for parliamentarians to accept in those committees. We believed that if we were providing government money for regional development we should have some say in how we encourage those corporations and facilities to set up in a particular area.
The senior bureaucracy in Ottawa wanted the amalgamation that took place when the Liberals got rid of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I suspect that it is some of those same bureaucrats who are responsible for successfully persuading the Conservative Government to integrate further and diminish the role of regional economic expansion within the new Department that is being established under legislation before the House.
Our Constitution requires that Parliament take regional development seriously. I do not believe we can do so if there is no longer a Standing Committee that studies that area. Even more important, we cannot do so without a specific government Department with that mandate.
It is interesting to note that just before the Liberal Government of the day demolished the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, a consultant's report which it had requested indicated the Government should proceed in the opposite direction. I have a copy of the report. It states that the mandate of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has been good but that it really needs to be expanded. It has to expand its role of communication and co-ordination with the other Departments.
The report went on to give examples of why it was important. That was a worth-while study. I have not been a great fan of consultants, as many people in the House well know. I have not been a great fan of various studies that Governments have done. I have not been a great fan of the hiring process in terms of how those people get their jobs either. However, that study made a lot of sense. It actually amplified what we had heard in the Standing Committee on Regional Economic Expansion when we went into Atlantic Canada, Quebec and western Canada.
What we heard from the people at that time was that they wanted an expanded role for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Rather than having to deal with two Departments they wanted one Department which would do a lot of the leg work, which had the authority and the emphasis within government to ensure that regional development occurred. As well, they wanted it to have the political muscle in Cabinet to make sure that individuals in other Departments did not stymie a good project.
That was what the people in Atlantic Canada and in the other parts of Canada called for. The Government rejected that. That is why I am asking through this motion that we indicate as the House of Commons that we want to see that process re-established. We want to be in a position to have a focus within Cabinet and within the House of Commons to ensure that the people in the regions are listened to, that the Government is in a position to act, and that the House of Commons and its Members will be in a position to monitor the activities of

the Government when it comes to regional development.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT LONG-TERM PLANNING FOR ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment and indeed as an Atlantic Canadian, thank the Hon. Member opposite for bringing this motion before the House and for providing us with an opportunity to talk about regional development needs in Atlantic Canada.
However, I would like to tell him that the Government has already formed a long-term regional planning capability for Atlantic Canada through the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency established on June 7, 1987. I might say that it is a lot more than a grant dispensing agency.
I would also like to tell the Hon. Member that this agency has a Minister sitting at the cabinet table. It has a senior Minister sitting at the cabinet table. It has a former DREE Minister sitting on its behalf at the cabinet table. He is a Minister of whom we think very highly. We are quite satisfied that our interests are extremely well looked after in that the Minister responsible for the administration of ACOA is the Minister looking after regional development in Atlantic Canada.
Furthermore, we are very pleased that we have not only this new agency which functions as a Department but that it is centred in Atlantic Canada where Atlantic Canadians can play the lead role in determining what it does and how it functions.
The agency as legislated by Parliament is a permanent Ministry which has the principal responsibility in the federal Government for planning, implementing and co-ordinating programs and activities in support of regional development in the Atlantic region, including the administration and delivery of a $1.05 billion budget in incremental funds. I would like to have all of that money in the South Shore, too.
Regional Development
I would like to point out that in announcing this agency on June 6, 1987, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stated, and I quote directly from his remarks on that occasion:
The agency will have a strong mandate for the co-ordination and planning of all federal activities contributing to the economic growth of the region, particularly procurement, training and skills development, job creation, technology infrastructure development and local investment promotion. It also will be directly responsible for federal small and medium sized business and industrial development policy and programs in the region, working in close co-operation with provincial Governments and with the private sector. Special efforts will be made to ensure Atlantic suppliers benefit fairly from federal procurement requirements.
The role of ACOA was embodied in Bill C-103 which was proclaimed last year. The object of the agency as stated in Section 12 of the legislation is: "to support and promote opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada, with particular emphasis on small and medium sized enterprises through policy, program and project development and implementation, and through advocacy of the interests of Atlantic Canada in national economic policy, program and project development and implementation".
The agency has been provided with significant powers in Section 13 of the Act, including that to formulate plans to support economic development in Atlantic Canada in concert with other federal Departments, in addition to other program powers.
ACOA is the result of a new decentralized approach to regional development.
The agency is served by a private sector advisory board which provides input to the impact of proposed policy and programs. It keeps ACOA management advised on current private sector concerns.
The ACOA headquarters is located in Moncton, New Brunswick. There are regional offices in each of the provincial capitals, as well as an office in Ottawa.
The key point is that this agency is based in Atlantic Canada where it can benefit from the needs, the aspirations, and indeed the wisdom of Atlantic Canadians.
With limited resources of approximately 320 person-years ACOA makes use of expertise available within the private sector and other levels of government in the delivery of its operations.

May 15, 1989
Regional Development
The Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is a strategic partnership with the people of Atlantic Canada in the renewal of the Atlantic entrepreneurial spirit. In pursuit of this mission ACOA has adopted several strategic long-term objectives. The first is a self-sustaining entrepreneurial culture. The second is more successful small and medium sized businesses. The third is more lasting employment opportunities. The fourth is increased earned incomes. The fifth is national policies and programs which reflect the strengths, aspirations, and opportunities of Atlantic Canada. The sixth is an expanding competitive economy.
The elements of the ACOA mandate and the powers embodied in the legislation will provide the agency with the necessary tools to implement its mission and work toward the following four stated objectives.
First, the ACOA action program is providing the resources to undertake strategic risk sharing with Atlantic entrepreneurs. By engaging in this type of relationship with its clients the agency is gaining valuable insight into the future directions of economic development within Atlantic Canada.
Second, the co-operation element of the mandate sees ACOA implementing a new concerted approach to shared federal-provincial regional development funding in Atlantic Canada.
Third, ACOA is mandated to co-ordinate federal policies and programs aimed at stimulating Atlantic Canada economic opportunities. This is resulting in more efficient use of federal regional development resources.
Fourth, ACOA is devoting a portion of its energies to the advocacy of Atlantic interests across the entire spectrum of national policies and programs, from federal procurement to regulations and legislation. The goal of this element is to alter some long-standing stereotypes regarding the region's ability to compete with national standards. That is why it is so important it is an Atlantic based agency.
By far the most impressive of ACOA's accomplishments to date has been the unprecedented reaction to
the agency's action program. Since it was introduced in February of 1988 applications to the program have run at approximately ten times the rate of previous regional development programs. This accelerated activity has translated into over 5,000 approved projects. The direct private sector investment generated by these initiatives will amount to over $2 billion. I know that at the present time there are 200 applications in the ACOA office from the South Shore alone. We have had over 100 applications approved. Quite frankly, jobs are being created on a daily basis. With the downturn in the fishing industry we need that right now.
For example, in my own riding, Harry Freeman and Son in Greenfield has created 19 jobs; Nova Woodcraft in Bridgewater has created 8 jobs; ABCO Plastics in Mahone Bay has created 12 jobs; and Neptune Leather Company in Clark's Harbour has created 25 jobs. That is a result of a program that is based in the region and understands its potential. The economic spin-offs from this investment are expected to inject at least $2.5 to $3 billion into the Atlantic economy.
The effects of this economic stimulation are already being measured in lowered unemployment rates and the creation of some 14,000 jobs in Atlantic Canada. From December, 1987, to December, 1988, Atlantic Canada registered an 11.4 per cent increase in new business establishments, compared to 10 per cent for all of Canada. In each of the Atlantic provinces, increases of between 8.9 per cent and 15.4 per cent were registered for capital expenditures during 1988, over the previous year.
In conclusion, clearly this Government has taken some very tangible steps to ensure the permanency of regional development initiatives in Atlantic Canada. To date, those initiatives are working. As we head into the crisis in the fishing industry, I know that we can look to this Government for substantial support to see that the self-reliance of Atlantic Canadians which has been the key to our success in the past will be the key to our success in the future.
May 15, 1989

subtopic: REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have this opportunity to speak on the motion put forward by my hon. friend. I am delighted that he is sponsoring something of this nature for the Atlantic region.
The advisability of providing long-term regional planning for the Atlantic region is certainly a subject that is near and dear to my heart. The mainstay of my riding of Bonavista-Trinity-Conception is very much the fishing industry. However, I am also constrained to report to the House that the last time I checked the figures, the average income was approximately $22,500. According to the latest figures, that puts it very close to the poverty level for this country.
One of the main issues that I considered to be a point of great importance during the election campaign, and certainly one of my campaign platforms, was the way to get things moving in Bonavista-Trinity-Conception. There is hardly any industry there. It is my wish as the Member of Parliament for the 91,000 people whom I represent not only to raise the profile of the fishing industry but also to try to get something moving in the area of diversification in other industries.
I am particularly interested in the area of tourism in Mr. Holtmann: Mr. Speaker, I would like the record to Newfoundland. All Hon. Members who have been to show that the Hon. Member for Portage-Interlake Newfoundland would agree that there is a tremendous abstained.	potential for tourism. Unfortunately, we have not been
May 15, 1989

able to realize the full potential of this tourist industry for a number of reasons.
Of course, one reason is that although we have been around since 1497 and long before that, it is only in the last two decades that the potential of the tourism industry in Newfoundland has been recognized. Last year I believe we took in just over $300 million in the tourism industry. A large part of that came from the riding of Bonavista-Trinity-Conception.
We need regional development funding in Newfoundland in order to survive. I certainly need it in the riding of Bonavista-Trinity-Conception in order to conceptualize and work on some of the ideas that I have put forward to my constituents.
As I stand in the House today, I am in receipt of some 13 submissions to ACOA. They range from tourism to secondary fishery processing. They include mining and the building of hotels and motels. These applications represent the whole gambit of what can be done in my riding to develop ideas that can fuel the engine of economic growth.
I am very much in support of these and am indeed working with ACOA to make sure they get off the ground and proceed at a reasonable pace so that we may see some action in the foreseeable future.
I wish to speak for a moment about ACOA. There is no question that ACOA has been very successful. I would bring to the attention of the House that in the first year of its creation in Newfoundland ACOA received somewhere in the vicinity of 1,300 applications. That will give Hon. Members some indication of how popular this agency is.
In addition to ACOA there are other subagreements. In my presentation on the Budget I spoke about some of these areas. I refer now to Economic Regional Development Agreements, commonly known as ERDAs. These are lumped in my mind with regional development because they are in fact regional development agreements. If they were added up we would see that their total number amounts to $6 billion. That is a great deal of money.
I believe that six ERDAs have been approved in Newfoundland. I believe that there is some work going on with respect to them. However, vis-a-vis my earlier comments, I am particularly interested in the agreement
Regional Development
for tourism which ran out on March 31 of this year. I know that there are one or two major projects under way and some of a lesser extent that depend very much on these agreements. In particular, the tourism agreement amounts to something in the vicinity of $21 million. That is a lot of money for some of the projects that we are trying to get under way in Newfoundland.
The projects range from a hospitality home development up to and including the building of hotels and motels, as well as tourist attractions, roadside tables, fireplaces and that sort of thing.
There is one other area to which I alluded in the House not too long ago which I will deal with now. It was when the Hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dick) was speaking on another issue. I made note of the fact that in my briefings with ACOA I was very impressed with the dedication of all the people from the very top down to the account executives. I was somewhat distressed to find-and I am really putting words into the mouths of the senior executives-that they would like to do more but were constrained from doing so because they did not have adequate staff.
Looking at it from the output end one would expect that more could be done. However, purely from the input end alone the going formula for an account of the ACOA types would be between 10 and 15 for an account executive. This would allow an account executive to look at the incoming submission, to counsel the individuals or the company that has sought advice, and to discuss the whole procedure with the company. The account executive could send these people out to other agencies to seek assistance. I think that 15 accounts per account executive would permit that. However, in the case of ACOA I am told that the number of accounts for each executive is somewhere in the vicinity of 40 to 50. That does not permit the proper counselling and the institutionalized machinery to allow the success to happen as quickly as it should.
It would be my hope and desire that the favourable consideration of this type of motion put forward by my colleague would go a great deal of the way toward helping Newfoundlanders and indeed the people from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception in these types of submissions to have a better feel for the regional development programs, ACOA, and the ERDAs, as well as a better understanding of what is there so that they can make application and better treatment when they make their application. In the long term there could be a

greater measure of success and a greater chance of success.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me this afternoon to be able to participate in this debate. I am particularly gratified that my friend opposite from Churchill has moved this motion. It shows a recognition of all parliamentarians of the particular need for regional development, particularly in the Atlantic. I am pleased as well to be able to follow my friend from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, a riding that neighbours mine. He is a gentleman who understands some of the problems that we face.
All Members of this House would share, I think, a common concern that regional development is important, that the creation of jobs and the enhancement of our economy is something to be strived for by all of us. I guess what the question inevitably comes down to is the most appropriate method for doing that, the best process to follow.
What disturbs me most about this motion is that the move that my hon. friend from Manitoba would like to take is regressive. It goes back to where we were before. It goes back to the times that did not work. The reason we have ACOA and its response stems from years of it does not work, they do not know what our problems are, they do not understand us in Ottawa.
The response of the Government was to say, as my hon. friend from the South Shore has said: "What we will do is we will set up an agency in the region staffed by people in the region who will make decisions on something that they know. There will be a quick and effective response". It is not just a money pot. The last thing we need in Atlantic Canada is just a money pot. I am not saying that the last thing we need is a money pot.
It is critical that ACOA continue to play a role that was set up some time ago with the creation of the Federal Economic Development Co-ordinator, the FEDC. That system involved the chief public servant in the region, the senior economic adviser to the Government. Those who wanted to deal with the Government had to deal
with the FEDC. It was the FEDC who was in a sense the seed of the vice-presidents of ACOA.
Tbday, that role continues to be played out. Today, we continue to have the primary source of advice not only to government in Ottawa but to other government Departments, to provincial Governments, to those who are doing business in the regions, coming from the senior person in the regional offices of ACOA. The decisions are not being made in Ottawa. The decisions are being made in the region. If they are not being made by the vice-presidents, they are being made by the board. That is the way it should be. That is why ACOA is successful.
My friend from Churchill said something on which I have to comment. I do not want to take up my whole time in responding to him. He talked about the needs of Members of Parliament. I respect the needs of Members of Parliament, being one a few short months myself with many needs. The key here is the needs of the people of Atlantic Canada. It is the needs of the people who want to create jobs, the people who want to create opportunities. The people I grew up with and went to school with in Atlantic Canada, particularly in Newfoundland, only ever wanted one thing. That was the opportunity to create for themselves and for their families and their communities those things that would develop their communities in the future-economic growth and employment.
ACOA today is very active. It has been hugely successful, based on its mandate to do two things. It is an agency that supports job creation and job development and encourages others to do the same by modernizing, expanding and protecting our jobs. It is also an agency that plays a leading role in the development of the economy.
To the end of the year ACOA in Newfoundland and Labrador has had economic activity under the Action Program. It has grown ten times over the three previous initiatives. IRDP and AEP, the Atlantic Enterprise Program, saw 100 projects in 1987. Since ACOA was set up 7,000 inquiries have been held into its programs, 2,316 applications were received and 1,061 approvals have been granted. Over 40 per cent of these were new businesses and 38.4 per cent were for expansions.
May 15, 1989

In Newfoundland and Labrador ACOA's activities are expected to generate 3,200 new jobs and help maintain more than 7,000 others. That is a total of over 10,000 jobs created and maintained in an area of very high unemployment.
In terms of dollars, in 1987 we saw $21.7 million in federal money under IRDP and AEP and the ERDAs. Last year, $134.3 million reached Newfoundland and Labrador through ACOA.
In the manufacturing sector-time is a problem here, there is so much to say-in the service sector, I would like to refer to my hon. friend for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception (Mr. Mifflin) who quite rightly points out that the tourism industry is one of great opportunity for all of us. It is something that is natural to our province. It is something that we can do well. It is something that can grow exponentially. It is one of the largest employers in this country and it has the potential to be one of the largest employers in Newfoundland and Labrador.
We have provided $18 million in the tourism industry alone. It is quite clearly one of the areas that will continue to attract great interest, and that ACOA continues to want to fund and move ahead.
Sixty per cent, or $112 million, of the total sectoral investment in 1988 in the manufacturing sector came from ACOA. Some $40 million of this went into modernizing the Newfoundland and Labrador fishery. Modernizing the fishery is critical because not only do we modernize and keep up to date, but we increase our capability of adding value to our raw product in the region, creating wealth and jobs, and maintaining the profits in the region as opposed to exporting them to other parts of this country, or to other countries. That is absolutely critical.
That is the future of the region. That is where ACOA comes into the process. That is why ACOA, as a body, is dealing day-to-day with all the federal Departments, with all of the provincial governments individually, and their departments, and with industry groups, with those that want to go out and create jobs and can play such a substantial role. That is where it all comes together in that focus that is so important to us over the next few years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to all of the previous speakers on this very timely subject. This is a subject veiy close to the hearts of all Atlantic Canadians because, as we all know, regional development programs are the lifeline of Atlantic Canada. It is an important economic tool for the cash-starved provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, P.E.I., and Newfoundland. Recent developments by this Government clearly show that it is either unaware of the problems of Atlantic Canadians, or it just does not care. There is no commitment.
From its inception in 1969, by the then Liberal Government, regional development has become a focal point of the federal Government. DREE was established specifically to address regional economic development. Since that time, it has deteriorated and today it no longer exists, nor does its predecessor DRIE.
Bill C-3, we note, will abolish the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and put the emphasis on economic development only in Ontario and Quebec. I feel that they do not need the help any more than do the Atlantic provinces.
From 1984 to 1988 the Government has cut back $2 billion in regional development. The recent Budget cut back an additional $2 billion. The Government has refused to renegotiate the expired ERDAs. It has cut back on transfer payments.
This shows the Government's insensitiveness towards the needs of Atlantic Canadians. My home province has millions of dollars in ERDAs waiting to be renegotiated. Presently, there are eight ERDAs totalling over $78 million that have expired or will be expiring this fiscal year. Prince Edward Island needs these agreements, as they touch on all facets of the Island economy, including transportation, agriculture, fisheries and tourism. Prince Edward Islanders are fully aware of the deficit problem that Canada is facing. We are more than willing to do our
share, Mr. Speaker, but our share is growing. What the Government has to realize is that it is tampering with the economic base of Atlantic Canada, an economic base that is solely dependent upon indigenous industries of which these ERDAs have been put into place to assist. Vital to Atlantic Canada's economy is transportation and fisheries. In fisheries, small craft harbour projects are being cut back. There has been added tax on fuel. There have been changes to the UIC program which is vital to this part of the country.
Transportation is the cornerstone of economic prosperity and this has been severely hammered. VIA Rail cutbacks, threats to kill the Atlantic freight subsidies, the direct flights of Air Canada and others to the major centres of Atlantic Canada are being cut. What about the base closures? The Government has severely cut back bases in Atlantic Canada. Whether some agree or not, the bases in Atlantic Canada and other parts of Canada were put there as regional development programs. This Government has not provided any viable economic alternatives.
My colleagues and I support this motion but I would also add that not only do we need a permanent ministry responsible for regional development but this ministry should be a super ministry with the power to veto or alter any intentions by this Government to hurt the long-term economic development and the economic prosperity of Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly my pleasure to speak on this motion today. I would just like to read it to clarify it. The motion is basically to provide "long-term regional planning for the Atlantic region through an established permanent ministry responsible for regional development".
As much as I appreciate the Hon. Member for Churchill's interest in Atlantic Canada, I believe it would be a big step backwards and a big mistake. In fact, ACOA in place now takes it one step further from regional to almost every area, through the Enterprise Cape Breton Program, the Pictou Economic Development Program, Cumberland Development Program, et cetera. Area by area ACOA gets it right down to the grassroots so the people involved in economic development at the very lowest level have a say in economic development and the proceeds from ACOA.
May 15, 1989

This Government has taken bold action, I think, in formulating a regional development policy which is based on a decentralized approach and nowhere is this approach working better than in Nova Scotia.
ACOA is working for and with Nova Scotians from Sydney to Yarmouth to create a deliberate path of entrepreneurial renewal.
ACOA is supporting the activities of entrepreneurs, both new or seasoned, by sharing financial risk, by supporting the activities of their business organizations, by acting as an advocate in Ottawa and by working with the provincial Government to take progressive new steps toward economic development.
In the space of only one year, from February, 1988 to February, 1989, ACOA has received 3,328 applications for assistance in Nova Scotia alone under the action program, through its Halifax office and its Enterprise Cape Breton office in Sydney. Nearly half of these have been approved. This has generated $623 million in growth in Nova Scotia.
Sectors of the economy assisted include manufacturing, the service industry, tourism and accommodation and resource industries.
ACOA risk-sharing has been distributed throughout the Province taking into account particular needs in certain areas. For example, in Cape Breton, ACOA delivers its programs through Enterprise Cape Breton. With headquarters in Sydney and an office in Port Hawkesbury, again, focused right on the grassroots, the people at the level in these areas make the decisions and help provide the information.
The Pictou Economic Development Fund was established in 1988 and has provided nearly $4 million in assistance to entrepreneurs in that region.
The recently established Cumberland development authority in my own riding is undertaking a number of activities in support of economic development in the county and is working hand in hand with municipalities and development commissions. A national program could not do this.
ACOA provides programs and assistance that are both regionally and provincially responsive but, most important, they are in tune with the Atlantic economy and Atlantic Canadian entrepreneurs.
Regional Development
ACOA recognizes that Nova Scotia has strengths upon which to build. It has the largest population of the four Atlantic provinces, a diverse economy and a number of favourable economic indicators.
Building on local strengths and opportunities is fundamental to success. Since the day of its announcement, ACOA has put the entrepreneur, the non-commercial research establishment and the business organization front and centre in its strategy to create economic strength and vitality. It has been working veiy well.
In 1988, ACOA contributed directly to the creation of 5,752 new jobs and the maintenance of 1,540 jobs. That broke all records by far, compared to national programs that were in place before. Let me mention a couple of examples. One is Seagull Pewterer and Silversmiths Ltd. in my own riding which currently employs a staff of 136, up from two employees. It expects to create 50 more jobs to end up with 186 by the end of the year as a result of an expansion from assistance and interest buy-down from ACOA.
Seagull Pewterer is located in a small town in a rural area and many of the 186 jobs that will be created have gone to young people. These young people would not have any opportunities for employment other than Seagull Pewterer in this location. They play an important role in the community and they are a good corporate citizen.
Another example is Sarsfield Foods Ltd. in Kentville, Nova Scotia. It is a maker of high quality, home-style frozen pies. The company which began on a kitchen table to add value to the owner's apple orchard, today makes 30,000 pies a day. Following an ACOA assisted expansion, the growing company will have a workforce of 75 employees. The company will also have a spin-off in the local fruit industries since Sarsfield will have greater requirements for locally grown fruit. Instead of shipping unprocessed products of apples and fruit, we now ship finished products and keep the jobs in Nova Scotia.
ACOA's work in Cape Breton is carried on through Enterprise Cape Breton. A new spirit of entrepreneurship is taking shape in that part of the Province and the climate for investment is improving. A recent example of this was the opening of the Cape Breton Wallcoverings. ACOA has assisted this company with an interest buydown and loan insurance.
A division of the St. Clair Paint and Wallpaper Corporation, Cape Breton Wallcoverings is projecting 1989 sales of $20 million. Sixty-five employees are now working at the plant and that figure will grow as additional equipment is installed.

May 15, 1989
Regional Development
In summary, I disagree with the motion before us to centralize our regional development programs. It is very important to keep it locally. We can contact the people we apply to now. We can talk to people. With national programs, the applications disappear in Ottawa or wherever the national office is. There is no contact, no way to find out where they are or the status of the applications.
The objectives for ACOA have been set, the commitment has been made and in Nova Scotia the process is under way and working. In my view, it is working better than a Ministry located outside the region as this motion proposes.
